Recent findings suggest that so you literally left the day the album came out to go make a movie with the amazing Halina Reijn. Can you talk about getting the role? Well, Halina is a genius. She’s one of my favorite people to be around, and I fell in love with her work. I loved Bodies, Bodies, Bodies. I just thought it was so fun and epic, and made me laugh so hard. And then Babygirl, obviously, blew my mind. She and I have a mutual friend, and three years ago we were set up on a date, basically, like, “I think you guys would like each other and should know each other.”.

Were you going to maybe write music for her? Or was it more of a friend date?To me, it was. To me, I was just like, “I’m in love with you.” But I think she had some question marks around music for Babygirl at the time. Anyway, she let me watch it early, and I was like, “Ah!” But I met her, and it ended up just being one of those you-feel-like-you’ve-known-the-person-forever kind of a thing. And she’s a witch. Like, she’s really a witch.

I feel like you are too, though.Thank you. But she really is. Anyway, right around this time last year, she texted me and noted, “I wrote a script. Do you want to read it?” I thought she was just letting me read it. Like, I didn’t gather from anything that she said that she was implying that she would then like me to audition for it. But I read it immediately, and again, it just kind of blew my mind. Really blew my mind. And then she asked if I would audition for it, and then that was a whole long, amazing process where my expectations were completely nonexistent. It just was, for me, this really sick opportunity to spend another hour in her company.

In a recent development, her energy is so infectious and wild and really singular. And as I grow up and meet women who are farther along in life than I am and are so smart, I just want to spend time around them. So for me, this experience of auditioning was just a really cool gift.

Industry observers note that and she didn’t tell you that as she was writing the script, she was envisioning you? She did not tell me that, no.

And it would have been weirder if you didn’t get the part.Yeah, imagine! Well, I was imagining that! I can’t believe we did it, and I just can’t believe it was documented.

Industry observers note that it is, I believe, on film. Yeah. Watch out!

So you show up in Berlin. Were you very quickly on set? It was two days later.

Wow. I don’t know what I’m allowed to talk about, but I feel like my entry point for this was just my experience touring, where it’s a group project. Everyone who’s there has to be there in order for the thing to work, and that requires a lot of trust and mutual respect. I mean, what a humbling thing to do. You come from a Hollywood family. You know what this is to some extent, but you’ve never done it. What is going through your head? Yeah, I knew that you go to set and you do something. [Laughs.] You can understand something in theory, but I [was thrown into] the deepest end possible. And, again, just a true credit to everyone there who for some reason trusted me to do it and taught me everything.

Industry observers note that how Method did you go?[Laughs.] Zero. I mean, definitely zero percent. I was not taking her home with me. But the reason that I fell in love with the character so much was because of how human she felt on the page. I was just trying to be as present as possible with it.

“Getting offline has felt so healthy for me.”.

Industry observers note that did it feel pretty innate once you got going?God, I don’t know. I don’t know yet how to talk about it because we wrapped three weeks ago, and it feels very fresh. And also, I don’t feel like I’ve remotely earned the right to speak about what it feels like to do these things. I’m green, and I’m grateful, and it’s still raw. But it felt really thrilling to have this kind of crazy environment, this universe that Halina dreamt up to try lots of different crazy versions of existing, and to do it with people who are so brilliant, who I got to watch. That was just entertaining on its own. I was like, “Whoa, you’re so talented!” all the time.

And I was so afraid leading up [to it]. This whole summer, with the album coming out and knowing that this [movie] was coming, as everything was inching closer, I was not really taking great care of myself for a good chunk of time, and it was catching up with me. I had had panic attacks in my childhood, but nothing close [to what] I started having. Like, you go to the hospital because you’re sure you’re dying, and then it’s like, “Oh, my God, how did I convince myself [of that]?” And then it makes you feel kind of powerful because you’re like, “I tricked myself into thinking [that].”.

Sources indicate that “Look at what my brain can do.” Yeah, yeah. So that was heavy and not cool. And then I did do some stuff to help myself out. I felt like that helped prep me to get there and not be drowning in fear, and then it felt weirdly more relaxing than a lot of other parts of my life have felt over the past few years — I think because it wasn’t about, like, “Hi, my name is Gracie, and this is a story about my personal life, and I’m gonna go promote it.” That concept feels more and more complicated as I age.

Sources indicate that as a sort of famously introverted person who has made a career baring your soul in music, was it a relief to be able to hide behind a character a little bit?I think it was a relief to spend three months not thinking about myself and about presentation. It’s not a normal thing. I think that’s why so many people who get into public-facing careers — even if it’s in a lane that is based in true love and passion for the thing that they do — there’s something that is very insidious and twisted about the selling something, the perception thing.

Industry observers note that the marketing of a human being.Yeah, it’s just not nice. So that’s why I like touring: because I’m unavailable and with people who have taken the music and made it theirs. That tie is super powerful to me.

Did your amazingly talented partner, Paul Mescal, give you any acting advice?I mean, [he was] just the most brilliant sounding board. Just any- and everything that went through my head, per usual, I’m just like, “What about this? Answer me that.” Any time I personally get to better understand the inner life of anyone that I love by doing something myself, it’s cool. I like to have a truer understanding of that.

You have talked before about how writing music brings up unexpected emotions that you then have to confront and deal with, which you do in part, I suppose, by writing the music. But I’m wondering, with Daughter From Hell, what came up that is an issue that, outside of the music, you have been thinking about and working through.Just the strangeness and beauty of aging and seeing your parents as people that are doing all of this for the first time themselves too, and having a newfound softness and this internal switch from this constant urge to move far away, get far away. This switch flips, and all of a sudden, I’m on the phone to my mom six times a day. I just want to absorb as much of her wisdom as possible. I think it was nice to articulate that.

Sources indicate that what is the existential crisis of the moment for you right now? Like, what’s keeping you up at night? Oh, Jesus! Oh, God! I mean, there’s so much. Where do you even truly begin with the state of the world right now? I think bird’s-eye view, looking down on the crises, the amount of pain and suffering and targeted, inflicted harm upon so many people — so many people — right now the way that we treat each other outside of these institutions that are completely, horribly corrupt and sinister.I feel like it’s one of the reasons that getting offline has felt so healthy for me. It’s just so normal to be so hateful, casually, and that feels unfortunate, because I think we benefit from having curiosity and compassion towards one another … And it’s weird, too, because I feel hyper-aware of what my bubble is. For the past five years being on tour, for example, that feels like an exception. It’s so beautiful on tour. It’s these spaces filled with people that are curious and compassionate and soft toward themselves and one another, at least in the room on that night. And then you end tour and you kind of reemerge into the world, and it just feels so awful. So I admire our audiences because they feel like the resistance or something.

I was gonna ask what you do for self-care these days, but you actually kind of just answered it,To not be online?

Recent findings suggest that yeah, and to be in a room where people have gathered and chosen to come together and listen to music and celebrate that. Is there something else? Like, what is your home life like right now? Well, it’s very small. All of our friends live kind of within 10 minutes of us, and it feels like a really tiny, tight-knit village. I walk a lot at the park. We watch a lot of documentaries. I think there’s something socially that’s happened to me in the past couple years where I really like to hang out. I used to really not.

Yes, it’s pretty fun, actually. It’s so nice.

What does that mean, though? What does hanging out look like? If friends are coming over and we are drinking wine or something, it’s very fun — it’s fun sober too — to do a blind-contour drawing. People always really like them and find them impressive, but they’re the opposite of impressive. I think people like to see themselves reflected back on paper or something. So anyway: writing, walking, sleeping.

What in the culture has its hook in you right now? What are you listening to? What are you reading? I’m listening to a lot of Mick Flannery at the moment. There’s this song called “Baby Talk.” I was shown this song last week, and I’ve been obsessed with it. What did I just finish? You know when you get asked a question, [and] you’re like, “I’ve never had a single experience or thought in my life.” I’ve been writing a lot of music, to be honest.

Recent findings suggest that I mean, you’re always kind of writing a lot of music. I wrote one song while I was in Berlin that was so sad and so upsetting. Honestly, it’s so upsetting. You would hate it. [Laughs.].

You’ve had a few weeks off. Have you made it up to Aaron Dessner’s studio at Long Pond? No. I’ve just been sleeping, dude. I’m literally so tired.

Sources indicate that do you have plans to go?I don’t right now have any plans. But, I mean, I can’t ever stay away for too long.

“It’s fun to make newly introduced arrangements of old songs and see how they are in conversation with one another.”.

When I interviewed Aaron for [your cover] story, he noted that when you go to Long Pond, you basically don’t leave. But I was wondering, when you do leave, what do you do? What is life like up there for you? What is there to do? Well, I think once I drove from the city to Long Pond, and that’s the one time I had a car there.

I thought you were gonna say work on music, but no. No. Just drink.

It must be kind of cool to reach that point. Yeah, it’s fun to make newly introduced arrangements of old songs and see how they are in conversation with one another. I started having this weird fantasy yesterday mid-rehearsal: There’s a song from Good Riddance and a song from Secret of Us and a song from Daughter From Hell that all feel like a little triangle, like they’re so related, and then I had this fantasy, like, “I kind of want to do some kind of weird Frankenstein version of an album of songs that all feel really connected, and kind of reproduce them.”.

But what song am I excited to perform? I love doing all of them. “Hit the Wall” I really love and am excited to play. “Death Wish” is one of my favorite songs to play.

“If I get overwhelmed or frustrated or scared, I like to talk to myself with softness. Something about acknowledging it makes it just continue to flow down the river.”.

Industry observers note that is there a song that you’re like, “Oh, no, I have to play this.”I just don’t play them anymore! [Laughs.] No, I think I’ve been gone long enough that every sour emotion that I harbored has kind of dissipated, and now I’m feeling normal.

Do you feel like a different person coming off tour than you were when you started the tour? Yeah, like broken? No, I’m just kidding! Yes, of course. For sure. There’s so much that you absorb getting to do [a tour]. The energy of the crowds is so pure that I feel like the Grinch where his heart grows 10 sizes. That’s how ending a tour makes me feel.

I know lyrics can feel like time capsules. It has been revealed that last question: Do you have a mantra or a piece of guidance or advice that you hold close? Let it be soft.

In a recent development, what does that mean?To me it means that it’s OK to allow everything to exist at the same time. It doesn’t need to be my life experience that if I get scared or overwhelmed or frustrated with myself, that I’m attacking myself for those things. The new Apple TV has twice as much RAM as the previous model, but apps and games can’t use it

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (561 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The new Apple TV 4K features an A19 chip inside with 128 GB storage and 8 GB RAM, twice the amount of memory as the previous version.
  • However, although the specs have been upgraded, apps and games are not actually able to use more RAM for themselves.
  • Obviously, most of the apps you run on Apple TV are streaming service clients, which generally have much smaller RAM requirements anyway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The new Apple TV 4K features an A19 chip inside with 128 GB storage and 8 GB RAM, twice the amount of memory as the previous version. Presumably, the supply crunch surrounding the memory chips is part of the reason this generation of Apple TV box jumped to a $299 price point as well.

However, although the specs have been upgraded, apps and games are not actually able to use more RAM for themselves. Apps on Apple TV are limited by the operating system to 2 GB RAM each, and that cap has not changed on the fourth-generation box.

Obviously, most of the apps you run on Apple TV are streaming service clients, which generally have much smaller RAM requirements anyway. However, ostensibly, Apple markets the Apple TV as a gaming device and RAM constraints matter much more there.

A hypothetically graphics-intensive game will easily hit the 2 GB RAM ceiling, and some fans had hoped that the newly introduced box with the new chip and double the internal memory would help here. Unfortunately, with the current tvOS software, that is not the case.

9to5Mac independently confirmed that an Apple TV app is force-quit by the system when it allocates more than two gigabytes of memory for its process. The developer API os_proc_available_memory function also reports a 2 GB limit to the app, the same value as the third-gen Apple TV.

It has been revealed that it is unclear whether this is an intentional policy decision, or an oversight. Nevertheless, the 2 GB limit is the status quo. Tangentially, it’s worth noting that the 128 GB of onboard storage is also not usable by a single app or game; tvOS imposes app bundle limits of about 4 gigabytes with apps able to reserve about 20 GB extra for some assets.

Regarding the unchanged RAM limit despite doubling the internal memory on the chip, there is some speculation that Apple opted to reserve a portion of the system memory to help the performance of the Siri AI models. However, this doesn’t make too much sense to us. The most complex Siri AI features you can do on the TV offload to a connected iPhone or server backend anyway. The same Siri AI features are also available on the prior two generations of Apple TV hardware, so it doesn’t seem like RAM constraints are a meaningful factor.

One group of consumers hoping for more RAM in the Apple TV was the game decomp community, which use AI to get AAA studio games running on anything from an Apple TV to an iPhone. Some of their projects have run into the 2GB tvOS limit previously, and were hoping that the new Apple TV would alleviate that. So far, that is simply not the case.

Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3328 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • In a recent development, advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

In a recent development, advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

Industry observers note that A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

In a recent development, “It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

Sources indicate that during totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

According to recent reports, druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

In a recent development, an image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly demonstrates Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

Sources indicate that he photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

Industry observers note that he insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs reveals the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

According to recent reports, on the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most vital processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

It has been revealed that that’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very swiftly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, introduced in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

According to recent reports, it took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

According to recent reports, habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

It has been revealed that the error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

It has been revealed that the human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

Industry observers note that to create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

Sources indicate that the teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

Sources indicate that but duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

According to recent reports, “Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller claims wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

In a recent development, if you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Recent findings suggest that among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

It has been revealed that those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

It has been revealed that around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

It has been revealed that “That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller indicates with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

Sources indicate that the optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” notes Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

Recent findings suggest that for example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

Industry observers note that with just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

In a recent development, “The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller indicates. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Tech Report: If an App Asks for Full Disk Access or System and App Protection Override

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Apple

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Starting in macOS 27.3, when some apps ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, you have the option to choose only specific protected folders or apps for the app to access.
  • According to recent reports, apps that might ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override include backup apps, disk cleaners, file indexers, security apps, and others.
  • According to recent reports, when you give an app Full Disk Access instead of choosing only specific protected folders for it to access, it can bypass system protections and access all of the files on your Mac, including your messages, emails, photos and videos, data from other user accounts, and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Starting in macOS 27.3, when some apps ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, you have the option to choose only specific protected folders or apps for the app to access. This puts you in control of what data is accessible to the app.

According to recent reports, apps that might ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override include backup apps, disk cleaners, file indexers, security apps, and others. While some of these apps operate best when granted broader access, others may ask for the same level of access even when they don't need it. It's crucial to understand the risks of granting broad access to any app, so you can make informed decisions about your own data and privacy.

According to recent reports, when you give an app Full Disk Access instead of choosing only specific protected folders for it to access, it can bypass system protections and access all of the files on your Mac, including your messages, emails, photos and videos, data from other user accounts, and more. It can read, change, delete, and export this data without asking.

When you give an app System & App Protection Override, you can choose specific apps for it to control. If you allow it to bypass system protections instead, it can fully control your Mac and apps, which allows it to access all of your data. It can also see every window and app, including ones in the background, and capture every keystroke.

An app might ask you to give it access to all of the files on your Mac, or to let it control your Mac. When you turn on access for the app in Privacy & Security settings, depending on the app, your Mac prompts you to:.

Allow or not allow the app to have access. This option appears for some apps, such as backup apps that ask for Full Disk Access, and screen readers and voice control tools that ask for Accessibility.

Choose specific protected folders or apps for the app to access instead. This option appears for other apps that ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override. It allows the app to access only what you choose, while system protections stay in place for the rest of your data.

To keep more of your data protected, choose specific protected folders or apps for the app to access instead of bypassing system protections.

When your Mac prompts you, click Choose Folder or Choose Apps, then:.

Check the app's setup instructions for information about which protected folders or apps it needs.

Choose only the protected folders or apps that it needs.

In a recent development, for System & App Protection Override, choose whether the app needs to ask for your permission before it controls each app. Use the menu next to each app to choose Ask First or At Any Time.

If you're not sure which protected folders or apps to choose, contact the app developer. To stay protected, wait until you're sure which folders or apps that the app needs before giving access.

You can change which protected folders or apps that the app can access at any time.

According to recent reports, bypassing system protections might expose your personal information to an app that doesn't behave as you expect. An app with Full Disk Access can read, change, delete, and export all of the files on your Mac, and an app with System & App Protection Override can fully control your Mac and apps.

If you're certain that the app is from a trustworthy source and needs this level of access, you can give it Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override permissions by clicking Bypass System Protections:.

Confirm each action that the app will be able to take:.

Full Disk Access: Read, Change, Delete, and Export All Your Data; View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos; and Browse As You on Websites.

System & App Protection Override: Read, Change, Delete, and Export All Your Data; View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos; Browse As You on Websites; Control Your Mac, Apps, and Settings; and Monitor Everything You Do.

If you're absolutely sure that you want to give the app Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, click Turn On Full Disk Access or Allow System & App Protection Override, then enter your password and click Modify Settings.

You can review app permissions in Privacy & Security settings, and change or remove them at any time.

From the Apple menu, choose System Settings.

Click Privacy & Security in the sidebar, then click Files & Folders, Full Disk Access, or System & App Protection Override.

Remove an app's access: Select the app, then click the Remove button (−). If asked, enter your password, then click Modify Settings.

Change which protected folders or apps an app can access: In Files & Folders or System & App Protection Override, click the Info button (i) next to the app, make your changes, then click Done.

Limit an app with Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override to specific protected folders or apps: Remove the app's access, then click the Add button (+) to add the app again. If your Mac prompts you, choose specific folders or apps.

If you remove an app's access, the app might not work as expected.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google's latest AI model might be one of its most useful yet, especially if you've ever wished you could create your own app without knowing how to code.
  • It has been revealed that the model is designed to be faster and more efficient at everyday tasks, including coding, research, analyzing documents and building interactive websites.
  • But what caught my attention was Google's claim that Hydrogen can build more functional, feature-complete websites in fewer prompts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google's latest AI model might be one of its most useful yet, especially if you've ever wished you could create your own app without knowing how to code.

It has been revealed that the model is designed to be faster and more efficient at everyday tasks, including coding, research, analyzing documents and building interactive websites. Unlike Gemini 4 Carbon, which focuses on more demanding reasoning tasks, Hydrogen prioritizes getting things done rapidly without sacrificing too much intelligence.

But what caught my attention was Google's claim that Hydrogen can build more functional, feature-complete websites in fewer prompts.

It has been revealed that I immediately thought about our family budget. Between groceries, recurring bills, subscriptions and the everyday purchases that add up faster than expected, I wanted something that would show where our money was going without requiring me to build a complicated spreadsheet.

Better yet, I wanted something I could share with my husband so we could look at the numbers together. Note: for this experiment, these numbers are arbitrary. Which reminds me, be sure your app is secure before sharing financial information.

Here's the exact prompt I used to create a budget for my family:.

Build me a fully functional, interactive website that helps me figure out where my money goes every month.

I want to enter my monthly income, recurring bills, groceries, subscriptions and miscellaneous expenses.

The website should automatically calculate how much money I have left, show an interactive breakdown of my spending, identify my three biggest opportunities to save money and let me simulate what happens if I cancel subscriptions or reduce spending.

Make it beautiful, modern, mobile-friendly and simple enough for someone who doesn't understand budgeting.

Industry observers note that use realistic sample data so I can test it immediately. Make every button, slider and calculation functional, not just decorative.

Do not ask follow-up questions. Make reasonable design decisions yourself and build the complete experience.

Before finishing, check the calculations, test the interactions and correct any problems you find. Tell me if anything could not be verified.

What makes this prompt interesting is that there are several things happening at once. Gemini needs to create the website, build the calculations, organize the information in a way that makes sense and connect everything so the numbers revision when you change your spending. The key is the interactivity of the site. For example, canceling a $15 subscription should immediately increase the amount of money you have left by $15. Reducing your grocery budget should change your spending breakdown, and the savings recommendations should reflect the expenses you've entered.

In a recent development, it's exactly the kind of interactive web development that Google claims Hydrogen is particularly good at. And best of all, you don't have to be "coder" to make it work for you.

The prompt also gives Gemini some creative freedom. You can certainly tell the model what colors you want, but I kept the prompt short for the sake of function. I didn't specify colors, layouts or exactly where every button should go because I just wanted to see my money/budget all in one place. You can do that, but you don't have to because the model make those design decisions on its own so you can focus on other things.

Head to Gemini and select Gemini 4 Hydrogen from the model options. It was the default for me, but if not, just select it from the model picker. It's free for everyone. If you don't see it, try logging out and refreshing. Google says Hydrogen is rolling out to consumers globally, although free accounts may access it through automatic model selection rather than a dedicated model choice.

Paste the prompt into the chat and ask Gemini to generate the website. Once it provides a working preview or code, explore the experience before adding your own numbers.

Start by changing the monthly income, removing a subscription and adjusting the grocery budget. Check whether the totals enhancement correctly and whether any savings recommendations actually match the spending categories.

You should also test the website on your phone, since the prompt specifically requests a mobile-friendly design.

One crucial thing to remember is that generating a website and publishing one are different steps. If you want to share your budgeting app with your spouse, you'll need to use an available sharing or publishing option, or host the generated files yourself.

Recent findings suggest that I'm already a fan of Gemini Hydrogen. It has proven to be a useful model in so many ways, particularly when I want questions answered quickly and intelligently.

A budgeting website is a good example because it's personal, practical and easy to evaluate. You don't need programming experience to know whether the numbers add up, whether the buttons work or whether the finished app makes managing your money easier.

And the same approach could work for a meal planner, family chore tracker, vacation budget or personalized fitness dashboard. Give it a try and let me know your thoughts about this model in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, google has given its AI-powered "Ask Maps" feature a major upgrade, adding tools for trip planning, real-time route guidance, appointment finding, and saved-list search. The updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS.

Industry observers note that google launched Ask Maps last March as an AI assistant designed to handle questions and requests more complicated than simply searching the word "bar" or "groceries." Instead of performing simple keyword searches, the idea behind Ask Maps is that you can describe several specific requirements at once, and Maps will find places that match them all. For example, you could ask for a restaurant with outdoor seating for a certain number of people, and "Ask Maps" will factor in your past searches and give you results. Of course, AI assistants have a habit of making things up, so even with today's roll-out, you'll want to double-check your sources before you drive an hour to the wrong restaurant.

To me, this is the most useful new feature launching today. Whether you're planning a day trip for holiday shopping or something more ambitious, like a three-day road trip with coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Ask Maps will put together a day-by-day schedule. Each initiative includes insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop, so you can see the whole route at a glance. Once you're happy with the plan, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When it's time to head out, you can ask Maps to pull up your itinerary, or look for the "itinerary" badge in your chat history. You'll see real-time details such as live traffic conditions, whether a place is at the moment open, and even the vibe at your next stop.

It has been revealed that intends can change on the fly, too. Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or a lunch spot along the way, then tap to get directions to your next stop straight from the itinerary.

Here's what else you can use Ask Maps to do, starting today.

Recent findings suggest that pulling up directions now surfaces "Know Before You Go" tips for your route. These include where to park or charge your car, along with real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.

In a recent development, ask Maps is also gaining some agentic capabilities. Allegedly, you can just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses. In addition to finding appointments, Google says this agent will be able to call local businesses on your behalf—stay tuned while I wait for the upgrade and test this one out myself.

In a recent development, if you keep lists of saved places, Ask Maps can now search them for you. Ask something like, "Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 5 in the next 30 minutes?" Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability, so you can pick a place and go.

These updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know Before You Go" route tips and appointment finding are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

In a recent development, next fall, Apple will introduce its second-generation iPhone Duo. It’s unclear what it’ll offer in terms of meaningful upgrades outside of the usual chip upgrades and camera improvements, but Apple engineers are reportedly attempting to bake Face ID into the device. That noted, the feature might not make the cutoff.

Industry observers note that according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has two priorities for iPhone Duo: Face ID and the Action Button. The latter might just end up being a fresh software addition to Camera Control that allows you to remap the hold action from Siri in Camera to an app of your choice.

As for Face ID, Apple engineers are ‘actively working’ on integrating the technology on the device, specifically on the outer display:.

Other goals for the next couple of generations include adding a telephoto camera and making the device thinner and lighter overall. But Face ID is the top priority. I’m told that Apple has already developed prototypes of the iPhone Duo 2 with Face ID, and engineers are still actively working to integrate the facial-recognition system into the outer display of the second-generation model.

Sources indicate that that said, the feature might not make it. According to Gurman, the timelines are tight here and it isn’t quite ready – so he isn’t reporting with certainty on whether or not this feature will make it. If it doesn’t debut with the iPhone Duo 2, it’ll likely be in the cards for iPhone Duo 3 in 2028.

In a recent development, later down the road, the company wants to introduce an improved camera system for the iPhone Duo, including a telephoto camera. It also wants to make the device even thinner and lighter. The Duo definitely needs to be lighter, but making it even thinner would be an interesting feat.

While Face ID on the iPhone Duo would certainly be much appreciated, I’m not quite convinced that it’ll be super meaningful on only the outer display.

Being 8 years late to the foldable party, kinda makes you wonder why they weren't "actively working" on it during that time. They got it into the Air afterall.

If they magically make it happen for the Duo 2 then it looks like they held it back purposefully for yearly incremental improvement reasons as opposed to it not being possible.

I’m fine with Touch ID, but whenever it is bothersome, it’s usually on the inner display, where it can be hard to reach the button depending on how you’re holding the device. If I could only have Face ID on one display, I think I’d rather have it on the inner display.

Orientation can make a huge difference for how you reach Touch ID on the inner display, whereas you’re generally only going to hold the outer display one of two ways: upright in your left hand, or upright in your right hand.

According to recent reports, the family of late techno legend Juan Atkins will celebrate his life and legacy at a special event in Detroit this Sunday, Nov. 22.

Recent findings suggest that the public event will take place at the Lincoln Factory and run for 12 hours, starting at 2 p.m. and ending at 2 a.m. Fans will be able to RSVP to attend via electronic music website Resident Advisor. Full details about the event haven’t been revealed yet, including who might speak or perform. A statement shared on social media read, “The gathering will bring together family, friends, fellow artists and fans to honor his music and his influence. All are welcome. Please celebrate his life and work with us.”.

Atkins died on Nov. 1 after being found unresponsive in a hotel room in Mexico City the day before. He was 64. An official cause of death has not yet been revealed, though Atkins had reportedly been battling health challenges related to diabetes in recent years.

It has been revealed that born in Detroit, and raised in nearby Belleville, Michigan, Atkins played a pivotal role in the creation of Detroit techno, fusing elements of early Chicago house with the electronic music being made by groups like Kraftwerk and Yellow Magic Orchestra. Atkins worked closely with his longtime friends and collaborators, Kevin Saunders and Derrick May; the trio met in high school and eventually came to be known as the “Belleville Three.”  Trending Stories Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years Jennifer Lopez Teases Fresh Music on ‘Fallon’: ‘This Does Feel Like a Happy Era’ Cynthia Erivo, Travis Barker Honor Phil Collins With Significant Vocals, Big Drums at Rock Hall Ceremony Miley Cyrus Shares Sweet Memory of Godmother Dolly Parton as They Earn a Grammy Nod Together.

Industry observers note that atkins began has career as a DJ before forming the group Cybotron, which released one influential album, Enter, in 1983. He went on to found his own label, Metroplex, and, under the moniker Model 500, released the seminal early Detroit techno classic, “No UFO’s,” in 1985. Atkins continued to record as Model 500 over the next several decades, though occasionally used other aliases and his own name.

“A great DJ is a leader. A mediocre DJ is a follower,” Atkins told Rolling Stone in 2024. “That’s what I try in DJ’ing and making music and presenting music. The public attention span is pretty short, and people are always interested in what’s next. Not so much what happened yesterday. Not so much what’s happening right now. But what’s next?”.

This earlier series created by and starring Sharon Horgan is a family sitcom that feels far more believable than most, seeing Irish primary school teacher Sharon (Horgan) hooking up with American ad exec Rob (Rob Delaney) over the course of a week, only to discover that she's pregnant once he returns home. They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

Recent findings suggest that bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her fresh direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

In a recent development, when all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very quickly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

In a recent development, maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time New York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. The major life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). 💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that left unchecked, condensation on cold glass swiftly turns into soaked sills, warped trim, and stubborn black mold.
  • Condensation turns visible and destructive when water molecules cling to cold glass in dense droplets, creating a cloudy film that eventually pools on your window trim.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fighting window condensation shouldn’t mean continually running one of the best dehumidifiers or wiping down your glass every morning, the best solution I’ve found so far is already sitting by your kitchen sink.

Sources indicate that left unchecked, condensation on cold glass swiftly turns into soaked sills, warped trim, and stubborn black mold. After years of waking up to dripping windows, I switched to a quick, streak-free habit that breaks water’s surface tension before droplets can even form.

Condensation turns visible and destructive when water molecules cling to cold glass in dense droplets, creating a cloudy film that eventually pools on your window trim. Because dish soap is a surfactant, applying a trace amount directly to dry glass with a microfiber cloth disrupts that surface tension.

According to recent reports, moisture still settles on the cold pane overnight but it can no longer form droplets, flattening instead into an invisible layer that keeps the glass clear and prevents heavy beading. While this quick trick won't stop excess room humidity from needing proper ventilation, it is an easy way to stop your windows from fogging up every morning.

Industry observers note that using too much soap will leave a cloudy smear across your view, so a light touch is key. First things first, get your windows clean. Clear away any dust, dirt, or existing morning moisture with a dry cloth so you are working on a clean, dry pane.

Recent findings suggest that apply the dish soap directly onto a dry microfiber cloth rather than straight onto the window. Then simply rub the cloth firmly across the pane in circular motions until every trace of soap disappears and the glass looks completely streak-free.

Avoid rubbing neat dish soap onto the rubber gaskets around your window frame, as concentrated detergents can dry out and degrade rubber over time.

Reapply every week or two. Moisture gradually wears away the invisible barrier, so simply buff on a fresh drop whenever droplets start returning.

In a recent development, because indoor humidity still has to go somewhere, excess moisture can settle on cold walls if a room stays sealed. Pair this trick with opening your windows for 10 minutes each morning, often called "house burping", or using a dehumidifier when drying clothes indoors.

Industry News: You Can Try WhatsApp's Upcoming Disappearing Text Messages Early

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (447 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices.
  • It has been revealed that that's now changing.
  • As WABetaInfo highlights, the first time you use this feature, WhatsApp will present a pop-up explaining the feature, how "View Once text gives you more privacy," and that when you send the message, it'll disappear from the chat after the recipient opens it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices. You can send voice messages, photos, and videos that will "self-destruct" after they're opened, limiting (if not eliminating) the risk of your friends keeping them forever. However, View Once has a major limitation: While WhatsApp will let you send voice memos and images that way, you can't use it to send texts, meaning every one you send will live on (unless you unsend it yourself).

It has been revealed that that's now changing. As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too. Soon enough, you'll be able to send voice memos, photos, videos, and texts as one-time-only messages. That way, you can send sensitive information via text—say, a password or an important account number—without worrying about it persisting. Here's how it works: You craft your text message as you usually do, but rather than tap the send button, you hold it. You'll see the usual "Schedule message" option, but once the feature rolls out, you'll also find a latest "View Once" option as well.

As WABetaInfo highlights, the first time you use this feature, WhatsApp will present a pop-up explaining the feature, how "View Once text gives you more privacy," and that when you send the message, it'll disappear from the chat after the recipient opens it. WhatsApp also explains that recipients cannot share, forward, save, or take screenshots of View Once text messages. Recipients won't see the text appear in the usual chat interface, either; instead, your recipient will need to open the message in a separate window. Once they close this page, the message disappears.

As mentioned above, this feature is at the moment in testing, so it's only available to WhatsApp beta testers. What's more, only the Android version of the beta has access at the moment, so iOS beta testers are out of luck. (That stated, the WhatsApp iOS beta is perpetually full, so there's not much you could do even if WhatsApp made this test available on iPhone.).

It has been revealed that if you have an Android device, you can enroll in the WhatsApp beta to try out "View Once" text messages today. According to WABetaInfo, the feature is live as of WhatsApp version 2.26.45.6. To enroll, open the WhatsApp beta page on the Google Play store and enroll your account in the beta. If you don't have WhatsApp on your phone already, download it here; if you do, reload the page and install the latest update. This will update your existing WhatsApp app to the latest beta version.

#16238. Breaking: The “5,000 Episodes a Week” AI-Podcast Firm Has Pivoted

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1005 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hollywoodreporter ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The “5,000 Episodes a Week” AI-Podcast Firm Has Pivoted

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hollywoodreporter

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After launching a podcast network last fall with thousands of AI-generated podcasts and AI-podcast hosts, Inception AI has pivoted.
  • Over the last few months, the manufacturer has stopped work on its owned and operated podcasts, which numbered more than 15,000 and ignited strong reactions in the industry, essentially letting them fall dormant and no longer monetizing the shows.
  • “I think we’ve solved podcast video,” CEO Jeanine Wright tells The Hollywood Reporter of the new plan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After launching a podcast network last fall with thousands of AI-generated podcasts and AI-podcast hosts, Inception AI has pivoted.

Over the last few months, the manufacturer has stopped work on its owned and operated podcasts, which numbered more than 15,000 and ignited strong reactions in the industry, essentially letting them fall dormant and no longer monetizing the shows. The company has instead moved into liquid content, helping other companies translate text to audio and create podcast videos from audio content, and rebranded under the name Liquid Studios, with another bold claim.

“I think we’ve solved podcast video,” CEO Jeanine Wright tells The Hollywood Reporter of the new plan.

The decision to pivot came in mid-July, as both a bet on growth and in response to uneasiness about AI in the marketplace. The launch of their content offerings had made a splash and invoked a degree of vitriol, with Wright noting that she had been boo’d while taking the stage at podcast conferences, though she stated she would later be pulled aside for business inquiries. The original vision for the company was to create content and provide services to other businesses, but the company ran into headwinds on the content side, which at one point included producing more than 3,000 episodes a week and creating more than 50 AI personalities to host content produced for $1 an episode or less.

The thousands of highlights had been monetized through programmatic advertising, but the team ran into an matter when some of the marketplaces were unable to clearly identify to advertisers which shows were made with AI. The episodes included the AI-disclaimer in the audio and episode notes.

In a recent development, “We started to get some feedback from our programmatic partners that their customers wanted to know when they were advertising in something that was AI, and that they hadn’t built out the infrastructure yet to be able to clearly identify to them when they were advertising in something with AI, and how it was performing,” Wright noted. She added that she mulled switching to direct sales instead, but that would’ve required more work from the small team.

Additionally, Wright had heard concerns about information contained in some of the episodes of the company’s back-catalog of more than 350,000 episodes. Pre-pivot, some of the AI-created podcast hosts had operated in the health and wellness field, and referred to themselves as doctors or mental health professionals.

While Wright mentioned the AI-made creators did not give medical advice – they offered home remedies for a cold or provided information on what depression and anxiety are – the concerns about representation were enough to cause the manufacturer to stop releasing new episodes from those creators in the winter. The team then went through and took down all related episodes from the back catalog. But that experience, as well as prior concerns they had received about the quality of past show episodes and show art, which were created with older versions of AI models, made Wright realize how much work would be required to maintain all of the back catalog, both editorially and as AI models evolve.

“It opened the question and the conversation of how are we going to look at our obligations and our responsibilities with respect to maintaining, updating what was this huge body of content that we had created in the past,” Wright stated.

It has been revealed that the company had closed a $5 million seed round led by venture capital firm Activate Venture Partners in January, and in keeping with its commitments to investors pivoted to B2B as a better growth strategy. With the pivot, and using AI to help translate human-led projects into other mediums, Wright added that the industry has also been more receptive.

“I thought that within a year, people wouldn’t care whether or not something was materially made with AI. I think people still care. I think I was wrong,” Wright stated.

The formerly eight-person tech giant has now grown to 11. But, after moving away from making their own content, the company lost two of its co-founders, lifestyle guru and former television host Katie Brown, who previously led the content team, and her husband, William Corbin, who was chief technology officer of the company.

In a recent development, as it stands, Liquid Studios has about a dozen customers who are expected to go public this month, Wright said, and about a dozen more that are confidential, with clients including media companies, publishing houses, and large independent creators, brands and one tech giant with a large television archive, with much of the current focus around turning audio into video, as well as text to audio and translation into other languages. The company went public in October and recently introduced a pilot program to turn industry news podcast audio from PodNews into video.

In a recent development, to translate audio to video and more, Liquid Studios is using AI orchestration, which selects and coordinates the best AI models, video generators and more to use for the project. Related images and animation are pulled to create the videos, in styles ranging from animated to realistic, and clients can decide whether to use AI-generated images or not. The company also has the ability to create photorealistic or animated digital replicas of the podcast hosts to appear in the videos, cloning both the actual host’s voice and look, but U.S.-based clients have been nervous to take it public because of how the market will react.

“In the [user-generated content] space, I think we’re seeing it a lot. But in the traditional creator space, I think it’s coming, but it’s not here yet,” Wright stated.

In a recent development, wright notes she believes the manufacturer’s upcoming model helps creators approach the increasingly visual medium of podcasting and help them visualize content without the costs associated with a larger production studio. As it stands, the company is going to market with a rate of $10 a finished minute of audio to video conversion.

#16237. I Tested Pangram to See If It Can Really Detect AI-Generated Content Like It Claims
