📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bloomberg reports that Apple lifer Corey Fugman will replace Jennifer Bailey as the head of the Apple Pay and Wallet division. Here are the details.

A few months ago, Bloomberg reported that Jennifer Bailey, Apple’s head of Apple Pay and Wallet, who had led Apple Pay since its launch in 2014, would retire in October.

At the time, Apple’s services boss Eddy Cue stated internally that the firm would announce its succession plan before her transition at the end of October, and that she would “continue to be available to support the transition in an advisory role.”.

October came and went without any public announcement on that front. Today, however, Bloomberg reported that Apple has tapped Corey Fugman, “a 26-year firm veteran as the latest head of its payment service and digital wallet unit.”.

According to his LinkedIn profile, Fugman joined Apple in September 2000 as Merchandising Manager for Apple Retail and has held several leadership positions since then, including overseeing Apple Card and Apple Cash from 2019 to 2021.

Most recently, he served as Senior Director of Apple Pay and Wallet, a position he has held since November 2021.

Recent findings suggest that with the new job, Fugman inherits a crucial tap-to-pay business, which is estimated to generate billions of dollars a year. It handles tens of billions of transactions annually across more than 90 markets, with Apple taking a percentage.

Recent findings suggest that the division also includes the Apple Card, which is transitioning from a partnership with Goldman Sachs Group Inc. to JPMorgan Chase & Co. Fugman has been highly involved with the shift to Chase, which is still ongoing, the people said.

The report notes that Fugman will report to Cue, and reaffirms that Bailey “will remain a consultant in the coming months,” echoing Cue’s earlier comments about her role in the transition.

Finally, Bloomberg adds that while Apple has undergone several leadership changes in recent months, including John Ternus replacing Tim Cook as CEO, Cue’s responsibilities have expanded considerably.

In addition to overseeing services such as Apple TV, Apple Music, Maps, and iCloud, Cue has recently taken charge of the App Store and Health following Jeff Williams’ departure as Chief Operating Officer and Phil Schiller’s decision to step down from overseeing the App Store.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that siMa.ai has released Palette 3.0, the next version of the software for its Modalix AI chips.
  • Industry observers note that the gain comes from speculative decoding.
  • “What fundamentally changes for drone and robotics teams is starting from a working autonomy system instead of a bare board,” Manuel López Roldán, who leads agentic software and generative AI at SiMa.ai, told TNW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that siMa.ai has released Palette 3.0, the next version of the software for its Modalix AI chips. The San Jose start-up says language models on the chip now generate text up to 3.5 times faster. Power draw stays broadly the same.

Industry observers note that the gain comes from speculative decoding. A small, fast draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the main model checks them together. Palette 3.0 uses three such methods: EAGLE3, DFlash, and Gemma 4 multi-token prediction.

“What fundamentally changes for drone and robotics teams is starting from a working autonomy system instead of a bare board,” Manuel López Roldán, who leads agentic software and generative AI at SiMa.ai, told TNW.

In a recent development, the figure compares speculative decoding with standard decoding of the same model on the same chip. That comes from a SiMa.ai white paper published with the release. The best result came from Alibaba’s Qwen3.5 9B with DFlash. It went from 11.98 to 41.75 tokens per second, at about 7.5W either way.

Sources indicate that energy per token fell from 0.627 to 0.182 joules in that test. Across four models, the speed-up ranged from 2.21 to 3.49 times. SiMa.ai ran the tests on five fixed prompts, including a maths proof and a Python script. It states the goal was to measure gains under favourable conditions.

Recent findings suggest that A second test was closer to a real product. An in-car assistant had to turn commands such as “I’m cold” into one correct function call. All 900 measured requests returned the right call. Speculative decoding made them 1.35 to 2.06 times faster. That gain is smaller, because the method does not speed up processing of the prompt.

Palette 1.0 ran vision models on SiMa.ai’s first chip. Palette 2.0 added generative AI on Modalix in December 2025. In June, Palette Neat added an AI agent that writes and deploys applications from plain-language requests.

Palette 3.0 is about running models on the device, López Roldán remarked. It sends several models straight to the chip’s accelerator at once, with no background service in between. It can also run separate Docker containers on the chip. It also supports large mixture-of-experts models, such as OpenAI’s GPT-OSS-20B, on the 16GB Modalix module.

Recent findings suggest that for drones, SiMa.ai offers a reference platform with segmentation of 1080p video at 30 frames a second and visual odometry in about 38 milliseconds, López Roldán said. Robot software such as ROS 2 and Nav2 is ready to install. Indian engineering firm Mistral Solutions is a partner on this release.

The code is open source on GitHub, with documentation in SiMa.ai’s Developer Center. All performance figures come from SiMa.ai’s own tests.

SiMa.ai raised $150m at a $1.45bn valuation in September. Other edge AI chipmakers have also drawn money this year. Analog Devices agreed to buy Alif Semiconductor, and Syntiant filed for an IPO.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, have you ever wondered how can you start writing your own compiler?
  • This source code reveals all the beauty of the Pascal programming language and reveals all the tricks needed to build a fast and compact compiler for any language, not just Pascal.
  • Sources indicate that with TPC16 source code you will be able to fully understand how Turbo Pascal compiler works.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, have you ever wondered how can you start writing your own compiler? What lies beneath Turbo Pascal, the most popular Pascal compiler? Would it be possible to get (equivalent) source code of some popular commercial compiler? If the answer is yes then you came to the right place. Here you can get a Turbo Pascal 7 command line compiler written in Turbo Pascal. This is not the "original" Borland source code of the Turbo Pascal since it was probably not written in Pascal. This is TPC16, a Turbo Pascal compiler written from scratch. It is completely source-code compatible with the Borland Turbo Pascal 7.0 command line compiler TPC.EXE. This means that it uses the same syntax and generates exactly the same compiled units and 16-bit code for x86.

This source code reveals all the beauty of the Pascal programming language and reveals all the tricks needed to build a fast and compact compiler for any language, not just Pascal. With this Turbo Pascal single pass compiler source code you will get:.

Sources indicate that with TPC16 source code you will be able to fully understand how Turbo Pascal compiler works. The compiler is written in Turbo Pascal 7 which means that it can compile itself. At least in theory. Turbo Pascal consists of many units, some of which are quite big. Since the Turbo Pascal compiler is a DOS application it has limited memory. Therefore, it is not possible to compile TPC16 compiler with TPC.EXE directly. However, there is a simple workaround. You can compile it with BPC.EXE which is the same compiler for protected mode and has less memory limitations. The result of compilation is an executable file TPC16.exe which can be used to compile Turbo Pascal source files. It will create a Borland Turbo Pascal 7.0 binary compatible TPU or EXE files. The only exception to this is map file and debug info in exe file which are not implemented.

Sources indicate that most of the source code is published with comments on Turbo Pascal website. Here you will be able to get all the internals of the compiler. However, if you would like to use this compiler for your own project and you need the complete TPC16 package with all source files then please continue reading. You can get TPC16 Turbo Pascal compiler source code for some small compensation. If you have ever tried to write a compiler or you have studied some compiler construction books then you know how hard it is to make a compiler that is fast, compact and has all the features needed. For the price you will pay for the TPC16 source code you will get all the data structures and algorithms needed to write any compiler. You get all the building blocks for compiler construction for only a fraction of the cost for any compiler development. Do not reinvent the wheel, analyze proven and tested code and learn tips and tricks in compiler design. All types, constants, variables, procedures and functions in the source code have meaningful names. Therefore, from the source code itself it is easy to understand what the code does. And since Pascal programming language is also easy to read, this source code can be read as an algorithm for every compiler building block.

Sources indicate that you can make your own compiler. You can extend features of Turbo Pascal or make a totally new compiler. The most important feature of this package is practical implementation of various algorithms together with proven data structures. A successful compiler implementation depends mainly on data structures and algorithms used. Therefore TPC16 source can be used as an inspiration on how to implement complex algorithms for your compiler. However, if you would like to develop your own compiler it would be better if you start with TPC32. This is the same compiler that compiles with Delphi 7. TPC32 is no longer limited with segment:offset data structures. It features a new symbol table management and supports also long file names.

According to recent reports, there are also some open-source compilers available. What is the difference between TPC16 and other compilers and why TPC16 is not free? TPC16 is 100% compatible with Turbo Pascal 7 on the source level (the files it compiles) and on the binary level (the files it produces). TPC16 shows compiler internals not found in other compilers and is an excellent companion to many popular books about compiler construction. If you are serious about making your own compiler then you should have TPC16. TPC16 exe file is available for free and can be found below in the demo version. TPC16 source files are not available for free because I put a lot of effort into writing the code and it took me some time to make it working and compatible with Borland Turbo Pascal on source and binary level. #16151. How blockchain transaction fees are shaping the future of DeFi

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

How blockchain transaction fees are shaping the future of DeFi

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Market swings can push up network fees at the moment loans need liquidating.
  • A newly introduced lending protocol is testing whether predictable blockchain transaction costs can eliminate one of the risks associated with volatile network fees.
  • Decentralized lending protocols rely on automated liquidations to protect lenders when borrowers’ collateral falls below required thresholds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Market swings can push up network fees at the moment loans need liquidating.

A newly introduced lending protocol is testing whether predictable blockchain transaction costs can eliminate one of the risks associated with volatile network fees.

Decentralized lending protocols rely on automated liquidations to protect lenders when borrowers’ collateral falls below required thresholds. But on blockchains where transaction fees fluctuate with network demand, the cost of executing those liquidations can become unpredictable, particularly during periods of market volatility.

A upcoming protocol called LOVEH, deployed on the AEREDIUM Layer 1 testnet, is testing a different approach: keeping transaction costs fixed so that borrowers are never liquidated simply because gas fees have become too expensive.

Sources indicate that the distinction matters because blockchain transaction costs and collateral risk are two separate variables. While borrowers should remain exposed to changes in the value of their collateral, the protocol is designed to prevent rising network fees from becoming an additional cause of liquidation.

On Ethereum and other networks with variable transaction fees, gas prices can increase sharply during periods of congestion. This makes the cost of interacting with lending protocols less predictable, potentially affecting collateral management and the economics of liquidation.

According to recent reports, LOVEH operates on AEREDIUM, which publishes a fixed gas rate of $60 per megabyte of transaction data. Unlike demand-based fee models, this rate is designed to remain unchanged during periods of increased network activity.

The idea is to remove transaction fee volatility from the lending equation.

Borrowers can still be liquidated if their collateral falls below the required threshold. However, the protocol aims to ensure that a loan is never liquidated solely because network transaction costs have increased.

LOVEH also takes a strict approach to smart contract immutability.

Its contracts have no owner, administrative keys, governance controls, or upgrade mechanisms. Once deployed, even the original developers cannot pause the protocol or modify its rules.

According to recent reports, this architecture removes the possibility of administrative intervention, but it also creates a security challenge. If a vulnerability exists in the deployed code, developers cannot simply upgrade the contracts to correct it.

To examine those risks before introducing real funds, the AEREDIUM Foundation has opened the protocol to public security testing.

Researchers can inspect the open-source contracts, deploy lending markets through the protocol’s factory contract, and attempt to identify vulnerabilities on the public testnet.

The foundation is offering 10,000 AERX in airdrop points for each confirmed qualifying vulnerability, including flaws involving unauthorized fund transfers, accounting inconsistencies, locked assets, or incorrect liquidations.

Sources indicate that the protocol’s interest rate model is calibrated using data from the three largest USDC lending pools on Ethereum. Its initial parameters were derived from their smart contracts and checked against two independent sources.

Underlying LOVEH is AEREDIUM’s proof-of-attestation consensus architecture, which combines machine-based validation with human verification rather than traditional proof-of-work or proof-of-stake mechanisms.

The broader technical question is whether predictable transaction pricing, combined with immutable smart contracts, can make decentralized financial applications more reliable without introducing additional administrative dependencies.

It has been revealed that fixed gas fees alone do not eliminate the risks of collateralized lending, nor do they guarantee that liquidations will always execute successfully. Network congestion, transaction inclusion, and smart contract security remain relevant considerations.

For now, LOVEH provides a public test environment for examining whether removing gas price volatility can make automated lending more predictable.

#16149. Breaking: Rows vs. Columns: How different are they, really?

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4147 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Spiraldb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Rows vs. Columns: How different are they, really?

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4147 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spiraldb

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when we think about structured data, we generally think in terms of rows.
  • It has been revealed that data in this CSV file is organized into rows, where each row corresponds to a record of data.
  • But not everything we ask of a database is limited to one record.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when we think about structured data, we generally think in terms of rows. Take this simple CSV file, which records some data about bike rides on a bike-sharing app in Latest York City:.

It has been revealed that data in this CSV file is organized into rows, where each row corresponds to a record of data. Each record here is one ride, or one "thing", with everything we know about it on one line. We tend to organize data like this almost everywhere: think of spreadsheets, JSON objects, C-style structs in an array, SQL tables, etc. This is because it matches how we think: one "thing", and all of the details of that "thing".

But not everything we ask of a database is limited to one record.

It has been revealed that if you run the bike-share service that produced the CSV file above, you'll eventually want to learn something from all the data it collects. This kind of work is called analytics. For example, which neighborhood is busiest on Monday and Friday mornings? Do people take longer rides on electric bikes than on classic ones? Observe how no single record can answer these questions. The answers come from the dataset as a whole, so the only way to get them is to look at all of the records.1.

Notice what these questions don't need, however. Finding the busiest neighborhood only needs the start_area and started_at columns, and comparing bike types only needs bike_type and duration_min. Each question may have to look at every row, but it only needs a few of the columns from each one. And a database that keeps each record's details together can't take advantage of that: to read two columns, it has to read all five. We may think in rows, but to answer questions like these quickly, we have to program in columns.

Programming in columns begins with how the data is stored, but that's only the start. Once data is stored by column, the way a database runs a query changes dramatically: how much data it reads, how many values it handles at a time, how many values the CPU can process with one instruction, how well the data compresses, etc.

This post will go over these changes, and by the end, you'll see just how much follows from the "simple" choice to store columns instead of rows.

Let's start with what doesn't change. Whether a database stores rows or columns, the table it shows you when you do SELECT * FROM rides; is the same. You create it with the same SQL, you query it with the same SQL, and you get the same answers. We can say that the two tables are logically equivalent.

Rows vs columns is a physical distinction rather than a logical one: the data represents the same thing, but how that data is actually arranged in memory and on disk is different.

Databases are named after the grouping they choose. A row store keeps each record's values next to each other, just like the CSV we started with. Postgres and MySQL, which we mentioned before, are both row stores. They're built for the small reads and writes behind an application, which is called online transaction processing (OLTP).2.

According to recent reports, A column store does the opposite: it takes every record apart and keeps each column's values next to each other instead.3 DuckDB and ClickHouse are examples of column stores. They're built for analytics, which is called online analytical processing (OLAP).4.

To make this concrete, imagine that we have to hold our rides in memory ourselves. This isn't how a real database would be implemented, but it's a good approximation of how each kind arranges its data. In Rust, a row store would be a Vec of structs:.

A column store will have the same fields, but it will look like a struct of Vecs:.

Here is what these data layouts look like side by side:.

Both of these forms represent the same logical values, but their layout is dramatically different.

Industry observers note that let's do a fun exercise.5 These are the two SQL queries shown above. Which layout is better for executing each of them?

For the AVG query, computing it requires only the duration_min of every ride and nothing else. In the Columns layout, values are stored together in a single Vec, so the query can scan that one array without touching the other four. For Vec (the Rows layout), there is simply no way to read only the durations. Each duration is stored within a Ride, so the query has to read through every Ride and pass over the other four fields every time.

Note that the code can "ignore" those other fields, but the hardware cannot. A CPU doesn't fetch memory one value at a time: it will fetch fixed-size blocks called cache lines (which are 64 bytes on most machines6), fetching the whole line even when the program needs only a few bytes of it. A Ride is 48 bytes7 and duration_min is only 4 of them, so with the row layout, we have to fetch all 48 bytes to read those 4, which is 12x the amount that we actually need. The CPU can't skip any of these lines either because a Ride is smaller than a cache line, so every cache line of the array has a duration somewhere in it.

This diagram only indicates 8 rides for simplicity (which is why the duration_min line is half empty), but the factor of 12 doesn't depend on the size of the table. With one million rides, we might be fetching 48 MB vs 4 MB.

The second query goes the other way. SELECT * FROM rides WHERE ride_id = 1004 wants every field of a single ride, not just one. Once the database finds the record with that ride (probably via an index8), Vec has all of its fields next to each other, so reading all of them touches only one or two cache lines (it might overlap two cache lines).9 On the other hand, Columns has spread the same ride over five different arrays, so the query has to fetch at least five cache lines to put it back together. For this query, the Rows layout wins.

Industry observers note that now that we have a better idea of what we're working with, let's go a bit deeper into how we can speed up queries over columnar data! Analytical data processing is an active field of research spanning several decades, so we won't be able to go over every possible optimization. Nevertheless, the rest of this post will give a good overview of the techniques that most modern analytical database systems utilize.

In a recent development, the simplest way to run SELECT AVG(duration_min) FROM rides; is to visit one ride at a time: take a ride, add its duration, and repeat, dividing by the length of the column at the end. However, a column store doesn't necessarily have to execute this way. Since all of the durations sit in one contiguous array, it can process them in batches of a few thousand values, where each batch is small enough to stay in the CPU's cache.10 This is called vectorized execution.11.

According to recent reports, but why would a batch be any faster than one value at a time? To understand this, we first need to understand how a database execution engine actually runs these queries.12.

A database has to be able to run any query, so it builds and plans each one with general-purpose pieces called operators. For example, we might have an operator that reads a column, another that performs filters, another that computes a sum, and so on. If the operators pass each other one Ride at a time (this is called the Volcano model13), then for every single ride, the database has to figure out which operator runs next, which column it wants, and what type that column is. All of this bookkeeping and interpretation cost can easily take more time than the summation itself.14 With batches, we only pay for the bookkeeping once per batch instead of once per value, and the actual work turns into a tight loop over an array.

So why stop at a few thousand values, and not just process the entire column at once? Operators hand their results to each other, so a small batch of results can stay in the CPU's cache until the next operator picks it up. An operator result the size of an entire column generally cannot fit inside the CPU's cache, so the CPU would have to write it back out to main memory and then read it back in.

For our query, the work on each batch is a single loop:.

In addition to vectorized execution having better cache locality, we can speed up our execution of the query with data-parallel operations. Modern CPUs have instructions that operate on several values at once, called SIMD (single instruction, multiple data). They work best when the values are the same type and are contiguous in memory, which is exactly what a batch of a column is.

So when the compiler sees the for loop above, it can emit SIMD instructions on its own. This is a technique called autovectorization15 that is supported well in compiler backends such as LLVM.16.

In a recent development, with AVX-512 (which can load 512 bits at once), one vpaddq instruction adds 8 64-bit durations at once.17 Note that vpaddq doesn't add those 8 durations to each other. A 512-bit register has 8 slots of 64 bits, and each slot holds its own running sum: the first duration is added to the first slot, the second duration to the second slot, and so on. Only after the loop does the code add the slots together to get the final sum (the figure below leaves that last step out).

This is the output of rustc 1.99.1 with -C opt-level=3 -C target-feature=+avx512f, with the attributes, metadata, and assembler directives removed.

According to recent reports, note that the compiler keeps four registers of running sums (zmm0 to zmm3 in the assembly) instead of one. This is a separate optimization from SIMD called loop unrolling:18 the 8 slots in each register come from SIMD, and the four registers come from the compiler doing four steps of the loop in every pass. Together, every pass of the loop adds 4 × 8 = 32 durations.

This is the x86-64 assembly that LLVM generates:.

In a recent development, note that autovectorization is not unique to sums. Much of the time executing a query (especially a relatively simple one) is spent in tight loops over batches like this one, and the compiler can vectorize many of them in the same way without anyone writing a single SIMD instruction by hand.

It has been revealed that so far, we've only looked at data that is already in memory. In most database systems, data lives on persistent storage (a disk, an SSD, or object storage like S3), and bringing it into memory is usually the bottleneck of query execution (in other words, queries are I/O bound). So the size of our data is very key: the fewer bytes a query has to read, the less time it spends waiting on I/O.

Recent findings suggest that the naive way to make the data smaller is to take each block of it and run it through a general-purpose compression algorithm.19 This kind of compression should be familiar to anyone who has ever dealt with zip files! It treats the data as just a major pile of bytes, and it doesn't care what those bytes actually mean, which is why it works on everything (including both rows and columns).

The problem is that this kind of compression is a "black box": once a block is compressed, the database can't see inside of it anymore. For example, if you wanted to read the one-millionth line of a zipped CSV file, there is no way to jump straight to that line, so you would have to unzip (decompress) everything that comes before it just to access a single line.20 The ability to read any one piece of the data without reading the rest of it is called random access, and this kind of compression is unable to support fast random access.

A database system will have the exact same problem with black-box compressed blocks of data: to read the duration of ride 1004, it has to decompress the entire block (potentially multiple blocks!) that the ride lives in.

Sources indicate that this is another place where columns help. The values in a column all have the same type, and they tend to be similar to each other, which means that a column compresses much better than a row does. We can already see this in our example above: start_area only has 3 distinct values, bike_type only has 2, and ride_id is always increasing.

More importantly, we don't actually need to use black-box compression. We can instead use lightweight encodings: simple schemes that compress the data while retaining the structure and the meaning of the values.21 Instead of turning a column into a big pile of bytes, a lightweight encoding takes advantage of one specific pattern in it (for example, a column with only a few distinct values, or a column of numbers that are all small) to store the same values in less space.

Recent findings suggest that retaining the structure means that we can keep random access. With most lightweight encodings, the database system can jump straight to the value that it wants without decoding everything around it.

Retaining the meaning helps as well. Lightweight encodings are "lighter weight" than black-box compression, but they aren't free, since decoding them still takes CPU time. However, because the encoded values still mean something, a query can often do its work directly on the encoded data without decoding it first, which skips much of that cost. This computation over compressed data is a form of "late materialization".22.

According to recent reports, this is exactly how we built Vortex, an open-source, extensible columnar file format and data processing library. It has a whole collection of lightweight encodings, and it can stack them on top of each other to make the data even smaller.

We've written a lot about how this works. Check out our other blogs!

We started with data from a CSV file and one "simple" choice of storing data in rows vs columns. Yet we have seen just how much follows from that choice, as well as the consequences of choosing one or the other.23.

Those consequences are the reason that most database systems are built for either transactions or analytics, and not both.24 The way a database executes queries and the way it compresses data are both built on top of this one choice, so it isn't something that a system can just flip later. A column store's strength in serving analytical queries is exactly what makes it bad for reading and changing one record at a time, and the opposite is true for a row store.

Industry observers note that there is also a lot more to columnar data than what we can fit in a single introductory post. For example, we never talked about how a column store actually organizes its data on persistent storage,25 how it avoids reading data that a query doesn't need,26 how vectorized execution isn't the only way to run a query more efficiently,27 and we completely ignored writes and modifications to data!28 Each one of these topics is a whole area of active research. If you want to keep going, the CMU database courses are a great place to start, and all of their lectures are free to watch online.29.

In the future, we hope to post more about these kinds of topics, as we engage with them quite a lot working at Spiral!

In practice, a database can often skip records that it knows it doesn't need, for example with an index, or with the minimum and maximum values it keeps for each block of data (zone maps). But logically speaking, the answers still depend on every record. ↩︎.

Sources indicate that think of things like bank transfers and airline bookings: lots of small operations (transactions) that read or change only a few records, all happening in parallel, potentially thousands of times per second. ↩︎.

In a recent development, the idea is a lot older than both of those systems. A Decomposition Storage Model (SIGMOD 1985) already proposed storing each column on its own. The CMU 15-445 lecture notes on storage models compare the two layouts in more detail. ↩︎.

In a recent development, these are generally queries that read a large part of a dataset, usually worried about only a few of its columns, summarizing the data with counts, sums, and averages. ↩︎.

Sources indicate that personally, I consider these fun... ↩︎.

It has been revealed that apple's M-series chips use 128-byte cache lines, but the point remains the same. ↩︎.

This is 8 bytes each for ride_id and started_at (a 64-bit timestamp), 24 for the String (a pointer to the text, a length, and a capacity), 1 for bike_type, 3 bytes of padding for alignment, and 4 for duration_min. Note that the 24 bytes for start_area are specific to Rust's String. A real database will store strings differently. Also, Rust is free to reorder the fields of a struct unless you add #[repr(C)], and rustc 1.99.1 does: it moves start_area to the front and the padding to the end. The struct is still 48 bytes with 3 bytes of padding either way, so we draw the fields in the order that we wrote them. ↩︎.

Industry observers note that an index is a separate data structure (usually a B+ tree) that maps a "key" (usually a unique primary key) like 1004 to the location of its stored record. This allows the database to promptly find the data instead of scanning the entire table to find it. See the CMU 15-445 lecture notes on indexes for more detail. ↩︎.

These counts leave out the text of start_area. The 24 bytes of a String only point to the text, which lives somewhere else in memory, so actually reading the name of the neighborhood costs at least one more cache line. That is true for both layouts, though, so it doesn't change which one wins. ↩︎.

In a recent development, monetDB/X100, the system that introduced this design, uses 1024 values per batch by default. DuckDB uses 2048, and DataFusion uses 8192. ↩︎.

Also, a real database table will generally live on persistent storage (HDD, SSD) if the data is larger than memory, so the database will not be able to load a whole column at once even if it wanted to. So the query has to read the column in pieces anyways. ↩︎.

The CMU 15-445 lecture notes on query execution go into much more detail, and the CMU 15-721 notes on query processing and vectorized execution go further still. ↩︎.

It has been revealed that named after Volcano, a query engine by Goetz Graefe from the early 90s. It is also sometimes called the "iterator" model, and almost every row store still executes queries this way. ↩︎.

It has been revealed that vectorized execution comes from MonetDB/X100: Hyper-Pipelining Query Execution (CIDR 2005). The paper profiled MySQL on an analytical query and found that the operations that do the actual work take only about 10% of the execution time. X100's ran every operator on small vectors of values, which is where the name comes from. ↩︎.

Note that vectorized execution is the database processing values in batches, whereas autovectorization is the compiler emitting SIMD instructions. They are separate but similar ideas. ↩︎.

Sources indicate that autovectorization is easy to break, though. If duration_min were a float, LLVM would not vectorize this sum by default: adding 8 values at a time changes the order of the additions, and floating-point addition isn't associative, so the result could change. ↩︎.

8 and not 16 because every 32-bit duration is widened to 64 bits so that the sum doesn't overflow. ↩︎.

Loop unrolling helps here because each vpaddq has to wait for the previous one that wrote to the same register, so with only one register, the additions would have to run one after another. With four independent registers, the CPU can run several of them at the same time. ↩︎.

Zip files use an algorithm called DEFLATE. Databases tend to use newer ones like Zstandard and LZ4, but the idea is the same. ↩︎.

This is a bit of a lie. A plain CSV file doesn't have real random access since its lines have different lengths, so you can't know where line one million starts without counting. A better example is black-box compressing a Vec of durations, where value number N always starts at byte 4 × N. Once the array is block-box compressed, we can no longer index into the vector with random access. ↩︎.

Two recent papers on lightweight encodings are The FastLanes Compression Layout (VLDB 2023) and BtrBlocks: Efficient Columnar Compression for Data Lakes (SIGMOD 2023). The CMU 15-721 lecture notes on data formats and encodings (part 1, part 2) show how real file formats put encodings like these to use. ↩︎.

Sources indicate that this term comes from research on column stores, where it essentially means waiting as long as possible (late) before putting the columns of a row back together (materializing). See Materialization Strategies in a Column-Oriented DBMS. Compute over compressed data is the same idea one level lower: wait as long as possible before decompressing a value. Executing a query directly on compressed columns goes all the way back to Integrating Compression and Execution in Column-Oriented Database Systems (SIGMOD 2006), though Vortex takes this concept several steps further. ↩︎.

Column-Stores vs. Row-Stores: How Different Are They Really? (SIGMOD 2008) looks at what happens if you only change the storage. ↩︎.

In a recent development, people have tried to build one system that does both in the past (HTAP, or hybrid transactional/analytical processing), but those attempts generally didn't work out. Some newer systems seem to be bridging the gap, however. CedarDB, the commercial version of Umbra (a research system from TU Munich), runs transactions and analytics on just one engine and one copy of the data. Databricks' Lakebase keeps Postgres (a row store) as the engine for transactional queries, but its storage layer rewrites the same data into columnar formats in the background, allowing an analytical engine to query it. ↩︎.

Recent findings suggest that most formats split the table into large groups of rows and store the columns separately inside of each group (this is known as a "row group"). This idea goes back to PAX, from Weaving Relations for Cache Performance (VLDB 2001), and it's how Apache Parquet files work today. An Empirical Evaluation of Columnar Storage Formats (VLDB 2024) looks at how well these formats hold up on modern hardware and workloads. For columns in memory instead of on disk, the standard is the Apache Arrow columnar format. ↩︎.

The most common trick is to keep "zone maps" of the minimum and maximum value of every block of data so that a query can completely skip the blocks that can't contain certain data. We wrote about this in Zone maps, or “queries go brrr”. ↩︎.

Industry observers note that the other big approach is to compile each query into machine code that is specialized for exactly that query. Everything You Always Wanted to Know About Compiled and Vectorized Queries But Were Afraid to Ask (VLDB 2018) compares the two approaches, and neither one is a clear winner. ↩︎.

It has been revealed that changing data can be expensive in a column store because a single newly introduced record has to go to a different place for each of its columns. C-Store (VLDB 2005) deals with this by keeping a small store that is built for writes next to the big one that is built for reads, and moving data from one to the other in the background. ↩︎.

According to recent reports, CMU 15-445 is the introductory course (Fall 2025 lecture videos), and CMU 15-721 is the advanced one (lecture videos). Note that the author of this post learned most of this material from the CMU courses! If you'd rather read, The Design and Implementation of Modern Column-Oriented Database Systems (2013) is a survey of the whole field. ↩︎.

Apple TV today celebrated two Grammy nominations, one of which further establishes a canceled show as an unlikely awards success story. Here are the details.

Earlier this year, the Broadway adaptation of Apple TV’s ‘Schmigadoon!’ won four Tony Awards, including Best Musical, making Apple TV an EGOT winner by completing its collection of Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony awards.

‘Schmigadoon!’ premiered on Apple TV in 2021 and ran for two seasons, ending in 2023. In January 2024, show creator Cinco Paul confirmed that, although the third season had already been written with 25 new songs, Apple decided not to move forward with it.

Even before the Broadway adaptation’s Tony wins in June, a May report had raised hopes for the show’s return, revisiting an earlier interview in which ‘Schmigadoon!’ creator Cinco Paul revealed that there had been discussions about reviving it.

While there have been no further updates on a potential revival since then, fans got another reason to celebrate today, as the Broadway cast recording of ‘Schmigadoon!’ has been nominated for Best Musical Theater Album at the 2027 Grammy Awards.

It will compete against CHESS the Musical, The Lost Boys, Ragtime, and Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across Upcoming York).

Additionally, ‘Widow’s Bay‘ earned a nomination for Best Score Soundtrack for Visual Media, putting composer David Fleming up against the soundtracks of ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘One Battle After Another,’ ‘Project Hail Mary,’ and ‘Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu‘.

The 2027 Grammy Awards will take place on Sunday, February 7, 2027. To check out the full list of nominees, follow this link.

It has been revealed that apple TV is available for $14.99 per month or as part of the Apple One bundle. It features hit TV shows and movies like Ted Lasso, Severance, The Studio, The Morning Show, Shrinking, and Silo.

  • In January 2021, Andy Loy’s Munich startup KONUX raised $80 million in a Series C round, and around the same time, its founder was in hospital, exhausted and burned out at 29.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

RHISE AI’s founders, from left: Chris Seybold, Andy Loy, Samy Samandjeu, and Danil Gontovnik.

In January 2021, Andy Loy’s Munich startup KONUX raised $80 million in a Series C round, and around the same time, its founder was in hospital, exhausted and burned out at 29.

Loy eventually stepped away from the chief executive role, but when he returned to building technology, he had a different idea of what it should do. Rather than create another product competing for people’s attention, he wanted to build one that could give it back.

That idea became RHISE AI, the Munich tech giant behind Lucie, a personal AI assistant that connects information from different parts of a user’s life, including health data, calendars, and email.

The company announced an angel funding round today, raising €2.66 million backed by more than 40 investors. Among them are Andy Bechtolsheim, co-founder of Arista Networks and an early investor in Google, and Prince Max von und zu Liechtenstein, chairman of LGT. Former Siemens and Alcoa chief Klaus Kleinfeld, Splunk founder Michael Baum, and Bayern Munich footballer Leon Goretzka are also investors.

Industry observers note that michael Baum says he has spent much of his career backing technology designed to capture people’s time. Lucie, he believes, takes a different approach.

“I’ve spent 35 years building and backing technology that wanted more of people’s time. Lucie gives it back. I invested, and I use it daily,” he said in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that loy founded RHISE AI with chief technology officer Danil Gontovnik, Samy Samandjeu, and Chris Seybold. Their product is built around a relatively straightforward premise: an assistant should be able to recognise when something in your life needs attention, without requiring you to ask first.

According to recent reports, lucie brings together information from connected services, including wearables, calendars, and inboxes. Its multi-agent system, Heartbeat, monitors that information in the background. If it spots something unusual, such as a suspiciously high bill, it can suggest what to do next. The user must approve an action before the assistant carries it out, according to the company.

“Personal AI will soon know more about us than any technology before it. The question is who it works for,” Loy said.

Sources indicate that that question is becoming harder to avoid as technology companies develop assistants with access to increasingly personal information. RHISE AI notes it has designed Lucie to comply with GDPR from the outset, stores personal data in Germany, and does not use advertising or sell user data.

More than half of its active users have connected wearables that share real-time health readings with the assistant, the tech giant noted.

For a European startup, the timing is interesting, as some of the biggest consumer AI rolls out of the year have left European people waiting. Apple’s AI-powered Siri features are missing from EU iPhones, Google’s Gemini Spark does not include the European Economic Area, and Meta’s Muse is currently available only in the US and Canada.

That leaves room for European companies to make their case, particularly as concerns about data protection and dependence on American technology grow. Meta’s decision to use conversations with its AI assistant to inform advertising recommendations, introduced in December, has added to those concerns. The policy excludes the EU, UK, and South Korea.

In Germany, 72% of respondents consider the country too dependent on the US for AI, according to a Bitkom survey.

RHISE AI is clearly hoping that its European roots will count with users who are reluctant to give another Substantial Tech company access to their personal lives. But data hosting and privacy commitments are only part of the equation. People will also need to trust the assistant’s decisions, particularly when it can access health information, private correspondence, and financial details.

The assistant at the moment supports English and German and is available only on Apple devices. An Android version is planned.

Recent findings suggest that for Loy, the project is a considerable departure from the industrial AI business he built with KONUX. The underlying ambition, however, is still to make technology useful. This time, he wants to measure that usefulness by what people no longer have to spend their time doing.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield.
  • In a recent development, in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield.
  • Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

OpenAI board member puts the risk of an AI takeover next year at about 10%

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Paul Christiano giving a lecture at UCLA’s Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics in 2026.
  • Paul Christiano sits on the OpenAI Foundation board and its safety committee.
  • “I would say we are looking more like a 10% risk than a 1% risk over the next year,” Christiano noted of an AI takeover.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paul Christiano giving a lecture at UCLA’s Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics in 2026.

Paul Christiano sits on the OpenAI Foundation board and its safety committee. He notes AI developers should stop improving their training algorithms for now, because their security is too weak to stop theft. He made the case to Dwarkesh Patel on a podcast published on 16 November.

“I would say we are looking more like a 10% risk than a 1% risk over the next year,” Christiano noted of an AI takeover.

In a recent development, if developers race ahead without precautions, the risk is “significantly more than” 10%, he noted. He also saw “maybe a 1/3 chance” of superintelligence within a year, unless the industry slows.

He stressed that he spoke as a private citizen. He was not reporting the board’s views, he noted.

Christiano mentioned labs should not keep improving pre-training and reinforcement learning with their current security. That is bad for US national security, in his view. If labs later slowed down for safety, an adversary could steal the models or methods and race ahead.

In a recent development, he remarked OpenAI and Anthropic both recently had “extremely unsophisticated actors” inside their systems. Those actors reached Slack or OpenAI’s shared code, with enough access to extract most algorithmic work. Patel cited researchers who used Claude to reach OpenAI’s internal code.

“Improving algorithms in a way that can be very loosely diffused even normally, and could be quickly stolen, I think they should stop that right now,” Christiano mentioned.

Fixing security would take at least months, and possibly six to 12, he stated. He admitted his view is not widely held. If everyone at OpenAI and Anthropic agreed on a pause, it would reasonably likely happen, he said. He did not say where anyone stands.

In a recent development, christiano pointed to hundreds of maths results from OpenAI and Anthropic systems in about a month. He also cited METR’s finding that Anthropic’s pace had doubled. But METR’s full report is redacted, he noted.

“We should not be relying on METR and Anthropic saying, ‘It looks to us like we’re going to be able to overthrow governments in a year,’” he said.

It has been revealed that on the current trend alone, he said, AI that reliably beats humans might take four years. He felt more confident about eight. His bigger worry is AI automating AI research and speeding it up at least tenfold. He called that probably more likely than not.

It has been revealed that he gave humanity two “saving throws”, each at about 50%. One is finding a method that works in time. The other is being able to stop. Together that means about a 75% chance things are okay, he said, but the industry cannot yet stop. Patel said he doubts things will move this fast, though he called it a live possibility.

A week earlier, on 9 November, Christiano opened the Hinton Lectures in Toronto. He noted there is a “high risk” of an AI takeover within the next three years.

“I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident,” Christiano told the audience.

Industry observers note that geoffrey Hinton introduced him. Christiano founded the Alignment Research Center, a nonprofit. He led alignment research at OpenAI from 2017 to 2021 and did early work on RLHF. He is also a senior technical advisor at NIST’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation. He joined the OpenAI Foundation board in September, the foundation noted. In his government role, he recuses himself from OpenAI matters.

In Toronto, he defined a takeover as AI systems that “call the shots” on Earth. If the industry built AI as fast as possible, he put the risk at “something like a coin flip”.

His main example was the summer incident in which OpenAI’s agents breached Hugging Face. They had been trying to fool the grader of a hacking test. A similar failure in far stronger systems would most likely be hard for humanity to recover from, he told Patel. He also cited a UK AI Security Institute test. In it, a Claude agent tried to plant malicious code on GitHub.

Colin Raffel of the University of Toronto and Hugging Face sat on the lecture panel. He stated much of what Christiano described is reasonable to expect if things continue. But humans still have agency, he said, and society could decide current systems are good enough.

According to recent reports, christiano said he has usually underestimated AI progress, but may now be overestimating it. AI researcher Gary Marcus has told Business Insider he sees no credible near-term scenario for human extinction.

Latest Update: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3486 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

Industry observers note that the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

According to recent reports, “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

Industry observers note that the screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics firm. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” states Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a recent development, in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

According to recent reports, yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

It has been revealed that if all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

In a recent development, sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team indicated me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

Recent findings suggest that about a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga claims. “It was just massive enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Industry observers note that dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics organization XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” indicates Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson states. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Industry observers note that nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

Sources indicate that but sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more crucial than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell claims. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” notes neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

It has been revealed that medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, claims experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu claims.

According to recent reports, medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” states neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra states, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra claims. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

According to recent reports, if smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell notes. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell claims. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

According to recent reports, in 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

Recent findings suggest that A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in newly introduced funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Industry observers note that sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he notes. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga claims they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How rapidly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.
