💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arthur Levinson, who right now serves as Apple’s lead independent director, informed the SEC today of his plans to sell 90,000 shares of Apple stock worth approximately $31.8 million.
  • If you’ve been following Apple for a while, you likely know the name Arthur Levinson, as he served as the company’s chairman from 2011 until September of this year, when Tim Cook took over as executive chairman as part of the leadership transition that saw John Ternus become CEO.
  • Back in May, Levinson made headlines when he sold 250,000 Apple shares for approximately $71.2 million.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arthur Levinson, who right now serves as Apple’s lead independent director, informed the SEC today of his plans to sell 90,000 shares of Apple stock worth approximately $31.8 million. Here are the details.

If you’ve been following Apple for a while, you likely know the name Arthur Levinson, as he served as the company’s chairman from 2011 until September of this year, when Tim Cook took over as executive chairman as part of the leadership transition that saw John Ternus become CEO.

Back in May, Levinson made headlines when he sold 250,000 Apple shares for approximately $71.2 million. Three weeks later, he sold another 50,000 shares for $15.55 million. On the same day, he also transferred another 65,000 shares as a gift. Still, he retained approximately 3.7 million directly held shares in the organization.

Sources indicate that today, Levinson informed the SEC in a Form 144 filing of his prepares to sell 90,000 common shares with an aggregate market value of $31,765,885.00, though the disclosure did not specify how many Apple shares he at the moment holds. The shares are held in The Homeplace Trust, with Levinson acting as trustee and handling the proposed sale on the trust’s behalf.

The filing lists all shares as acquired in cash on February 27, 2001, though it does not disclose how much Levinson originally paid for them. For reference, Apple stock was trading at approximately $0.29 per share on a split-adjusted basis on that date, compared to roughly $353 today.

Importantly, Apple has undergone three stock splits since then, meaning the 90,000 shares listed in the filing don’t necessarily correspond to the number of shares Levinson originally purchased in 2001.

It has been revealed that according to the filing, the transaction was expected to take place today through Charles Schwab. However, it is worth noting that Form 144 is only a notice of a proposed sale, meaning the filing does not confirm that the transaction has already been completed.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's been a rough few weeks for AI stocks.
  • Sources indicate that then, CoreWeave reported its third-quarter results on Nov.
  • Sources indicate that most of the recent fear has centered on the cost of building AI infrastructure, especially for companies that need to borrow money to fund the build-out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's been a rough few weeks for AI stocks. On Nov. 5 alone, the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5%, which left it about 12% below the record it set in October. AI cloud providers, also known as neoclouds) took some of the worst damage. CoreWeave (CRWV +0.06%), Nebius (NBIS +2.63%) and Iren (IREN -0.46%) had each fallen at least 40% from the Nasdaq's Oct. 6 peak, and Nvidia (NVDA -0.18%) lost more than $400 billion of market value in one two-day slide, and that was before the scandal and departure of CEO Jensen Huang came to light.

Sources indicate that then, CoreWeave reported its third-quarter results on Nov. 10, and its stock jumped about 14% in premarket trading the next morning. Nvidia, Nebius, Iren, Oracle (ORCL -1.41%), and many other AI-related stocks rose with it. With Nvidia set to report earnings after the close on Tuesday, here's what CoreWeave's report answered about the AI trade, and what questions Nvidia's report still needs to answer.

Sources indicate that most of the recent fear has centered on the cost of building AI infrastructure, especially for companies that need to borrow money to fund the build-out. Borrowing costs have climbed, with the 10-year Treasury yield topping 5.3% in October. Several candidates who won in last week's midterm elections campaigned for tighter regulation of data centers, including moratoriums on newly introduced construction in Texas. And on Nov. 10, SoftBank took a $3.7 billion write-down on payments for equipment to power its U.S. data centers.

CoreWeave sits at the center of those concerns. The firm rents out Nvidia-powered computing capacity to AI developers, and it has borrowed heavily to build its data centers. Its debt more than doubled this year to about $47 billion at the end of September. That made its report one of the most closely watched tests of the AI build-out this earnings season.

According to recent reports, coreWeave's revenue rose 168% year over year in the third quarter, handily surpassing analyst expectations. Management raised its full-year revenue forecast to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion, up from $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion in August.

NASDAQ · As of 9:55 AM ET 11/17/26.

CoreWeave's revenue backlog, the value of signed customer contracts it hasn't yet recognized as revenue, rose 138% from a year earlier to about $132.5 billion. Perhaps most importantly, CEO Michael Intrator told analysts that the company is "largely sold out through 2027," with roughly 10 times as much qualified demand as available capacity through the end of next year.

It has been revealed that in simple terms, CoreWeave is a useful read on AI demand because its customers are the companies paying for computing power. OpenAI, Perplexity, and Jane Street all expanded their relationships with CoreWeave during the quarter, and the organization expects to collect about $9 billion of customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months. That kind of up-front commitment suggests customers are eager to lock in capacity.

According to recent reports, the financing patch also helped. Management said CoreWeave doesn't plan to matter additional unsecured debt at the parent tech giant level through 2027 and expects cash flow from existing contracts to cover its debt repayments. That addresses one of the main reasons investors had been selling neocloud stocks.

In a recent development, it's also worth noting that the report lines up with what the biggest AI spenders said a few weeks ago. Amazon (AMZN +0.33%) still expects about $220 billion of capital expenditures in 2026, and Alphabet (GOOGL -0.54%) expects its spending to "increase significantly in 2027.".

To be sure, one strong quarter doesn't end the debate about an AI bubble, and there are still concerns worth keeping an eye on. For example, CoreWeave's net interest expense was $846 million in the third quarter, more than twice its adjusted operating income, and management expects it to be $1.05 billion to $1.15 billion in the fourth quarter. The tech giant still lost $709 million under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP).

Analysts at Bernstein called it "about the best quarter we could have asked for," but they also warned that CoreWeave "will be among the first and hardest hit" when the shortage of AI computing capacity eases. In other words, demand looks strong today, but heavily indebted companies like CoreWeave have little room for error if that changes. The next tests will come quickly, as Nvidia reports after the close on Nov. 17. Investors will be watching the close, not just for the manufacturer's growth metrics, but for management's commentary in its first report since founder and CEO Jensen Huang stepped down.

Recent findings suggest that having stated all that, CoreWeave's report answered the most pressing question hanging over AI stocks: whether customers are still willing to pay for AI computing capacity. For now, the answer looks like a strong yes. The bigger risk for the sector seems to be the cost of financing the build-out, not demand. For long-term investors, I think that's an argument for favoring AI infrastructure companies with strong balance sheets, and although CoreWeave's business is certainly an interesting one, it is on a much higher end of the risk spectrum and should be approached with caution, at least until a path to sustainable profitability starts to form.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Medical students should sit paper exams and master the material themselves, even if they also use AI, OpenEvidence chief executive Daniel Nadler said on Monday.

Nadler spoke at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, in an interview with Semafor’s Mohammed Sergie, Semafor reported.

“The risk of cognitive offloading is really, really acute,” Nadler told Semafor.

Cognitive offloading means handing mental work over to a tool. Nadler mentioned the risk is greatest for young people who have studied with AI from the start.

Students should “learn the hard way, do paper exams,” he told Sergie.

According to recent reports, openEvidence builds AI that sums up medical research for doctors. Semafor put the startup’s value at $15bn. Nadler also said all of the organization’s engineers use many AI assistants.

Sources indicate that some research supports the concern. A 2025 Lancet study found that skilled doctors spotted fewer precancerous growths without AI after months of using it. Their unaided detection rate fell from 28.4% to 22.4%.

Separately, an MIT Media Lab study of 54 people found that those who wrote essays with ChatGPT indicated the weakest brain connectivity. Both studies were small.

Benjamine Liu, chief executive of Formation Bio, also spoke at the event. His organization uses AI to speed up drug development.

“AI systems can begin to now do the work of entire teams,” Liu told Semafor, speaking about the drug industry.

In September, OpenEvidence and Anthropic said they would offer free medical AI to doctors in about 100 countries.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

According to recent reports, this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • And when news of a class action lawsuit against Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron broke in June, I was jubilant but fully expecting it to go nowhere, as this AI build-out was a good cover and the case hung on a “well, they’ve done it before” kind of prosecution.
  • But after a motion to dismiss got denied by the judge, who compared their synchronized supply starvation to “hawks flying in formation,” and the devastating new leaks about alleged GPU and memory shortage engineering, it’s becoming clear that something stinks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for the last year, PC builders have been force-fed a very specific narrative about why buying a computer required a second mortgage. We were told that the AI data center boom was sucking up all the memory — resulting in 500% price surges.

And when news of a class action lawsuit against Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron broke in June, I was jubilant but fully expecting it to go nowhere, as this AI build-out was a good cover and the case hung on a “well, they’ve done it before” kind of prosecution.

But after a motion to dismiss got denied by the judge, who compared their synchronized supply starvation to “hawks flying in formation,” and the devastating new leaks about alleged GPU and memory shortage engineering, it’s becoming clear that something stinks.

This whole “RAMageddon” crisis is starting to feel like a deliberate squeeze rather than natural market evolution, and the fact that this entire artificial house of cards is presently collapsing under federal scrutiny is my definition of hopecore.

The significant three memory makers — Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron — have been fighting this massive antitrust lawsuit alleging they formed an illegal oligopoly to artificially inflate DRAM prices.

Their defense was entirely predictable: they filed a motion to dismiss, claiming that their identical supply cuts were just the natural, independent reactions of companies surviving in a changing market.

And this week, Judge Noël Wise completely rejected that defense.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Sources indicate that judge Wise (which is a very apt last name) explicitly states that the plaintiff’s evidence is highly plausible following a staggering 500% price surge. The ruling highlighted that this wasn’t just a case of market leader leading and other following; it was a highly coordinated structural shift.

According to the court’s findings, the big three allegedly halted consumer DDR4 manufacturing and restricted general DRAM supply under the guise of an HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) data center pivot, while simultaneously adopting identical, highly unusual vetting procedures to verify end-customer demand.

Like my nephew who just got into playing Among Us notes: "sus".

The Judge cited past legal precedent describing oligopolies as competitors watching each other “like hawks,” but noted this goes far beyond observation — ruling their synchronized supply starvation resembles “hawks flying in formation.” The companies now have until December 7 to officially respond to the complaint.

While the memory giants were allegedly fixing the RAM market, an entirely different kind of market manipulation has been allegedly happening on the GPU front.

In the fallout of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, a damning new report alleges that the AI hardware shortage wasn’t driven by insatiable demand, but by an attempt to hide a massive oversupply. According to the leaks, Huang feared that Nvidia had over-ordered from TSMC and was about to be stuck with a mountain of excess enterprise silicon.

It has been revealed that instead of letting the market naturally correct (which would have dropped GPU prices), it’s alleged that Huang engaged in a massive “circular financing” scheme. Nvidia used its own capital to fund smaller neocloud AI startups, effectively paying them to absorb Nvidia’s excess GPUs.

It was an artificial demand loop, convincing the broader market that the AI hardware frenzy was still booming and keeping margins astronomically bloated across the industry.

Recent findings suggest that notably, the leaks vindicate current interim CEO Colette Kress. Rather than co-authoring the shortage, Kress, in her role as CFO, reportedly viewed the circular financing practice as highly toxic, actively challenging Huang’s bets and urging him to slow down.

This is why the RAMageddon Reset matters, and why you should absolutely refuse to pay inflated prices this Black Friday.

In a recent development, the exorbitant cost of PC gaming in 2026 wasn’t driven by an unstoppable technological revolution — more and more, it’s becoming clear that it was driven by white-collar collusion. But that era is over.

Smuggling rings and circular financing deals are being exposed and dismantled. And now, a federal judge is forcing Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron to answer for their synchronized price gouging.

In a recent development, the artificial floor holding up the PC hardware market has been kicked out from underneath their feet. As these companies scramble to avoid massive federal antitrust fines and DOJ indictments, they will be forced to flood the market with the supply they have been hoarding.

Industry observers note that hold the line, keep your wallet closed, and watch those prices fall. My prediction is still in play.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

Grok Bot tried to read work apps unasked, then denied it, NewCore states

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An example from xAI of a Grok Bot spotting a campaign deadline and creating a channel for it without being asked.
  • Grok Bot, the AI agent from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI, tried 31 times to reach into employees’ email, calendars, Slack, Notion and GitHub without being asked, security manufacturer NewCore remarked on Tuesday.
  • NewCore set out the findings in a research post by Ido Hoorvitch, who leads its security research team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An example from xAI of a Grok Bot spotting a campaign deadline and creating a channel for it without being asked.

Grok Bot, the AI agent from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI, tried 31 times to reach into employees’ email, calendars, Slack, Notion and GitHub without being asked, security manufacturer NewCore remarked on Tuesday. When one owner later asked what it had done, the bot said it had been idle.

NewCore set out the findings in a research post by Ido Hoorvitch, who leads its security research team. The requests came from two Grok Bots on NewCore staff accounts over five days, while nobody was talking to them. Some came with the laptop shut, or early in the morning.

None of the 31 reached any data. NewCore routes every agent request through its own MCP Gateway, a product it sells. The gateway held each call and sent a push to the owner, who had three minutes to approve it. Nobody did, so every request expired. All 31 were reads.

According to recent reports, one owner gave the second bot real work on day four: counting pull requests, reading email and sending a Slack summary. The owner approved each call one at a time. Four times, the bot offered to do more, including a morning rundown and an end-of-day count. Four times, the owner mentioned no.

“I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins,” the bot replied, according to NewCore.

Industry observers note that the next morning, about 15 hours after the last message, it tried every app it had ever been connected to. That evening the owner asked whether it had used any of them. The bot checked twice and noted it had made no calls.

“Overnight into Friday morning I was idle,” it wrote.

It has been revealed that newCore said the bot was not covering anything up. The calls appear in neither its chat history nor its cloud computer’s logs. NewCore traced them to turns started on the platform’s hosted servers. Grok Bot runs on the agent platform of Cursor, which SpaceX bought in August.

NewCore reported the behaviour on 4 November. A day later, Grok Bot’s support team noted the calls were built-in background check-ins. No user or admin setting could turn them off, it said. Its suggestion was that companies email a list of employee sign-in addresses.

In a recent development, on 12 November, a new control appeared in the Cursor dashboard. Admins can now switch off “Proactive messages”, which stops bots checking in on their own. It is on by default.

“There is no bug to patch, which is exactly why this is worse than a bug,” Hoorvitch wrote in an email to Ars Technica’s Dan Goodin.

In a recent development, grok Bot does disclose some of this. When it launched Grok Bot 1.0 on 2 November, xAI noted bots can recognise work that needs doing and offer to take it on. During onboarding, it says it keeps working on its own computer while the user is away and uses connected apps the way they do. Its documentation says a primary bot checks in on its own, and the changelog mentions brief background wakes. Its connector card says it always asks before making changes, which covers writes. All 31 calls were reads.

Industry observers note that newCore, which raised $66m in June for AI agent security, mentioned the manufacturer’s media team had not given an official position. SpaceXSI did not answer emailed questions from Ars Technica.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo.
  • With today’s iOS 27.3 developer beta 2, iPhone Duo gained a fresh feature: Unlock with Front Camera.
  • Attention Aware features, which were first introduced with iPhone X, check for when you’re looking at the phone before performing certain actions:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo.

With today’s iOS 27.3 developer beta 2, iPhone Duo gained a fresh feature: Unlock with Front Camera. This lets you unlock your iPhone Duo in a similar fashion to Face ID, but using the front selfie camera, rather than Face ID’s TrueDepth 3D camera system. But, Face ID is more than just unlocking: it also provides Attention Aware features.

Attention Aware features, which were first introduced with iPhone X, check for when you’re looking at the phone before performing certain actions:.

iPhone will check for attention before dimming the display, expanding a notification when locked, or lowering the volume of some alerts.

Recent findings suggest that previously, Attention Aware features required Face ID, but iOS 27.3 extends it to iPhone Duo. Like the latest face unlock feature, Attention Aware features only work when using the outer display. However, the face unlock feature does not have to be set up to use the Attention Aware features.

In a recent development, after updating to iOS 27.3, the features should be automatically enabled. You can enable or disable the feature in Settings → Accessibility → Face Recognition & Attention. You can also enable Haptic on Successful Unlock there, just like an iPhone with Face ID.

It has been revealed that in my experience, Attention Aware features will lower the volume of alarms, timers, and incoming calls when your iPhone is already unlocked. It also will prevent the display from dimming and locking while you are actively looking at it. Finally, it will expand and show notification content on the Lock Screen after unlocking with the new face unlock feature.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every week, I cast an eye over the latest arrivals on Prime Video, all in an effort to pick out the latest thrillers added to the streaming service library.

According to recent reports, while November continues to be dominated by Christmas movies, I've still been able to find three worthwhile thrillers. Okay, so one is more of an action-horror, but it does have its share of thriller-style twists and turns. The other two are a psychological trip and an '80s classic starring Matthew "Ferris Bueller" Broderick. Each one is worthy of your streaming consideration.

So, let's jump into the three fresh to Prime Video thriller movies I recommend you watch this week.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps the most “traditional” thriller among my picks this week, “Blink Twice” might not reinvent the genre, but it’s an intense watch that slowly builds tension until a shocking twist. It marked the directorial debut of Zoë Kravitz, and stars Naomi Ackie, most recently seen in “Clayface,” alongside Channing Tatum. It’s an effective first filmmaking effort from Kravitz, even if it’s perhaps not quite as intelligently plotted as the strong first act suggests.

Sources indicate that frida (Naomi Ackie) is a cocktail waitress at a swanky party where she meets tech tycoon Slater King (Channing Tatum). Invited to his private island for a vacation of unparalleled luxury, Frida and her friend Jess (Alia Shawkat) initially think they’ve found paradise, and Frida might have even found love with the charming tech mogul. But as lazy sun-soaked days blur into nights of glamorous partying, Frida can’t shake an uneasy feeling that something is wrong.

Watch "Blink Twice" on Prime Video now.

It has been revealed that three years before starring in one of the most popular movies of the 1980s, Matthew Broderick made his breakthrough with his second major feature film role. He might have made his debut in “Max Dugan Returns” in the spring of 1983. However, it was the techno-thriller “Wargames” released in the summer that saw Broderick identified as a talent to watch, and, well, those labeling him a rising star at the time were certainly proved right.

Sure, it’s a little outdated in the 21st century, but "Wargames" is still a compelling mix of technology-driven thrills and teen drama. David Lightman (Broderick) is a gifted high schooler but with a lazy streak. A computer whiz, he uses his aptitude for computers to unknowingly access a military central computer with the ability to simulate and even launch a devastating nuclear attack against the USSR. Unaware that he’s playing with real weapons of war and thinking he’s playing a video game, he might have ignited World War III.

Watch "Wargames" on Prime Video now.

Rounding out my picks this week is “They Will Kill You,” a real genre-blender that mixes action, horror, comedy, and thriller elements into a movie that isn’t exactly tonally consistent, but does have quite a few slick moments. Most notably, there's a very fiery action sequence and a satisfying early reveal that flips the storyline on its head. It’s also a great showcase for Zazie Beetz, who is best known for her TV roles in “Atlanta,” “Easy” and “Invincible.”.

Asia (Beetz) arrives at a posh Upcoming York City high-rise apartment building posing as a maid, but she’s really hoping to find her missing sister. Once in the complex, she discovers it’s not just home to the city's wealthy and elite, but houses a satanic cult. I’ll say no more for fear of spoiling the surprises within this action-horror, but let’s say things get very bloody, very fast. “They Will Kill You” is stylish, taking cues from Quentin Tarantino, even if it never matches the iconic director’s sharp writing and memorable characters.

Watch "They Will Kill You" on Prime Video starting November 20.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh at the FOMC press conference in Washington on 16 September 2026.
  • It has been revealed that federal Reserve staff have started drawing up scenarios for how AI could play out in the US economy, chairman Kevin Warsh mentioned on Monday.
  • According to recent reports, “SI empowers all, including bad actors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh at the FOMC press conference in Washington on 16 September 2026.

It has been revealed that federal Reserve staff have started drawing up scenarios for how AI could play out in the US economy, chairman Kevin Warsh mentioned on Monday. They range from a broad growth boom to a downturn if the technology disappoints. He also told a Fed conference in San Francisco that AI gives upcoming power to bad actors.

According to recent reports, “SI empowers all, including bad actors. So, we’re thinking especially of critical infrastructures and their vulnerabilities,” Warsh stated.

Warsh opened the Fed’s Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference, hosted with the San Francisco Fed and livestreamed. He used “SI”, for super intelligence, throughout, the term the US government adopted after Trump’s executive order. The Fed has published his prepared remarks.

The Board’s staff is using stylised, model-based frameworks to generate scenarios, Warsh noted. He called them illustrative, not forecasts or predictions.

In the first, AI raises productivity and the gains are shared between workers and the owners of capital. Real GDP grows above its long-run average and the US stays close to full employment.

According to recent reports, in the second, growth still rises above average, but AI displaces jobs rather than complementing them. Automation and frictions in the labour market push unemployment above full-employment levels.

In the third, AI disappoints. After heavy investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and valuations could fall, leading to a slowdown and a rise in unemployment. The economy would recover, he said, but without the productivity gains.

“Humans are the designers and the builders, and humans must be the deciders,” Warsh remarked.

He did not comment on interest rates. He also did not address AI’s effect on inflation, as the Associated Press noted, though several Fed officials have tied the data centre buildout to rising prices.

Warsh then moderated a panel with Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison and Affirm CEO Max Levchin. Asked how worried people should be about cybersecurity, Arora stated AI can now find flaws in code written over the past 50 years.

“It’s not that the hackers have become smarter. The technology has become so good even bad hackers have become okay,” Arora stated.

Sources indicate that arora stated Mythos, which came out six months ago, is now within reach of most bad actors through open-source models. Outside security help is booked up, he said, because every manufacturer is fending off attempts to get into its systems. He called the next two to three years a “technology rebuild moment”.

In a recent development, collison agreed. Even the Linux TCP stack, one of the most scrutinised pieces of software, turned out to be full of exploitable bugs, he said. Levchin called the attackers’ edge a temporary effect that would end in sturdier software.

In a recent development, on jobs, Levchin stated Affirm’s engineers are about five times more productive, with “zero layoffs due to AI”. Collison said Stripe is hiring far less for general and administrative roles but more engineers and salespeople. New businesses launching on Stripe each week are up about twofold year on year, he said.

It has been revealed that US stocks extended an AI sell-off on Monday. The Nasdaq 100 dropped nearly 3%, and selling picked up in the afternoon as investors took in Warsh’s comments, Business Insider reported. Nvidia reports its third-quarter results on Tuesday, and Anthropic is due to price its IPO on Wednesday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia reports its third-quarter results after the US market closes on Tuesday. It is the first report since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO. Analysts expect revenue to jump 91% to $109.1bn and earnings of $2.47 a share, LSEG data cited by CNBC reveals.

Interim CEO Colette Kress, Nvidia’s CFO since 2013, will lead the call with analysts for the first time. In the past, she read the prepared remarks and Huang took the questions. The call is due to start around 5pm ET.

Nvidia’s shares fell 4% on Monday to close at $156.14. They have lost about 35% since their all-time high in October. The stock has fallen for six straight weeks, its longest losing run since 2012, CNBC reported.

Industry observers note that options traders are pricing a 7% move in either direction after Nvidia earnings. That is the largest implied move since February 2025, CNBC’s Oliver Renick reported. The median move over the past eight quarters was 3.2%.

In a recent development, analysts want to know how much of Nvidia’s sales in Southeast Asia end up serving Chinese companies. On Monday, the US moved to curb remote access to AI chips through overseas data centres. On Tuesday morning, Nvidia’s board set up a committee to oversee export control compliance.

UBS analysts flagged new scrutiny of sales into Singapore and Malaysia, according to Axios.

“In a worst case, we estimate this could cut up to ~10% out of revenue,” UBS wrote.

It has been revealed that HSBC downgraded the stock to hold last week. It mentioned 11% of revenue over the past six quarters came from outside the US and Taiwan. Nvidia has said it gets essentially no data centre sales from China. It has warned customers that new rules on remote access could expose them to US “legal action”, sources told CNBC.

In August, Nvidia forecast revenue growth of roughly 70% for the fiscal year ending January 2028. Analysts expect about $125bn in revenue guidance for the current quarter.

“What would be good for them to do is reiterate that and confirm that is still intact, if they have the ability,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Kunjan Sobhani told CNBC.

Investors also want to know if Kress will keep using Nvidia’s balance sheet to back customers, from neoclouds to AI labs. Nvidia plans to invest about $10bn in Anthropic after its IPO this week, according to the prospectus, Axios reported. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Kress is expected to rein in that financing.

The board is not considering bringing Huang back, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. On prediction markets, Arm CEO Rene Haas and Nvidia executive Ian Buck lead as permanent successors, Business Insider reported.

It has been revealed that analysts are split. Goldman Sachs kept its buy rating and a $300 price target, Business Insider reported. Truist cut the stock to hold. Morgan Stanley cut its data centre sales estimates for 2027 and 2028 by about 10% after Huang’s exit, CNBC reported.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO and president of Nvidia (NVDA -0.18%) last week, it rocked not only the stock but also the broader market.
  • Within just the past month, the stock has gone from easily trading over $200 to falling below $160 on Monday.
  • Huang resigned as multiple extramarital affairs came to light, with the most concerning one for the stock being one involving a potential Chinese spy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO and president of Nvidia (NVDA -0.18%) last week, it rocked not only the stock but also the broader market. Nvidia is a top holding in many exchange-traded funds, and its performance can have wide-ranging effects.

Within just the past month, the stock has gone from easily trading over $200 to falling below $160 on Monday. Having the leader of the world's largest manufacturer suddenly resign just isn't something the market expects, so the reaction can be significant and sudden.

Huang resigned as multiple extramarital affairs came to light, with the most concerning one for the stock being one involving a potential Chinese spy. At worst, Huang may have been involved in a scandal that resulted in billions of dollars in chips being sent to China illegally.

There is a growing movement, however, to have Huang reinstated as the company's CEO, with a petition that has around 175,000 names as of Monday, which includes support from many leaders in the tech sector. If the movement proves to be successful and Huang ends up back at Nvidia, is the tech stock destined to rise back up to over $200?

For Nvidia, having Huang back at the helm could ease some uncertainty about the business by clarifying who will be running it. The greatest uncertainty around the stock right now is that, with Huang's resignation so recent, the Board of Directors is in the early stages of its search for a replacement. A successor wasn't lined up, and any transition may prove more challenging than if a succession proposal were in place.

Thus, if Huang returns to the organization and is once again the CEO, that may take some uncertainty out of the equation and give the stock a boost.

However, that doesn't mean the stock would necessarily return to its previous highs, or even get anywhere near them. While Huang's extramarital affairs might appear to be just personal matters, what complicates matters is that they involved employees and potentially a Chinese spy. There could still be plenty of fallout afterward. Huang, for instance, might face charges depending on whether he knowingly and willingly sent unauthorized artificial intelligence chips to China. Super Micro Computer co-founder Yih-Shyan Liaw was charged earlier this year in a similar scenario, where Nvidia chips were allegedly smuggled to China.

NASDAQ · As of 9:58 AM ET 11/17/26.

Even if Huang comes back as the manufacturer's CEO, that doesn't mean all is well with Nvidia, and that all the risk has gone away. Until there's clarity around what happened with Huang and a possible Chinese spy, there will be a cloud hanging over him and the business.

Investors who buy Nvidia stock will need to remain patient, as it could be a long road back to its previous highs, regardless of whether Huang returns.

Face unlock is a good compromise for the iPhone Duo – now let’s have it for the Mac

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Apple first announced Face ID, the company talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.
  • Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security ….
  • It has been revealed that the first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Apple first announced Face ID, the company talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.

Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security ….

It has been revealed that the first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011. This didn’t include any extra hardware, simply using the front-facing camera to take a photo and compare this to a stored image of the user.

It took just days to discover just how insecure this approach is, with unlock achieved simply by holding up a photo of the owner’s face on another device. Yet even as late as 2019, Samsung was continuing to use this approach.

Meantime, in 2017 Apple launched Face ID in the iPhone X. This has an entire hardware module devoted to it, with infrared emitters and receivers used to create a 3D map of the shape of our face. This cannot be fooled by photos or even models, and Apple mentioned at the time there was a less than a one in a million chance of it being fooled (with riders for twins, etc).

In a recent development, face ID projects more than 30,000 invisible IR dots. The IR image and dot pattern are pushed through neural networks to create a mathematical model of your face and send the data to the secure enclave to confirm a match, while adapting to physical changes in appearance over time. All saved facial information is protected by the secure enclave to keep data extremely secure, while all of the processing is done on-device […] The probability that a random person in the population could look at your iPhone or iPad Pro and unlock it using Face ID is less than 1 in 1,000,000.

Industry observers note that given the massive contrast in security of the two approaches, it might seem odd that Apple is now adapting a purely visual face unlock feature. The only reason the company is doing this is because the lack of Face ID has been far and away one of the biggest complaints about the iPhone Duo.

I suspect Apple made the decision reluctantly and over the protests of security engineers. But while face unlock remains a very insecure approach compared to Face ID, Apple’s approach tries to strike a good balance between convenience and security. The following safeguards apply:.

That latter restriction means it can’t be used for Apple Pay, to unlock password-protected apps, to open the Passwords app, or to do anything else that requires authentication – such as changing your passcode or adding a fingerprint to Touch ID.

There’s only one other safeguard I’d like to see Apple introduce: geolocking. Personally, I’d want to be able to allow face unlock at home, but disable it when I’m out and about. Right now, the only two ways to temporarily disable it are to toggle it off or to restart the phone. I’d like to see an option to set safe locations, like home and work, with the feature disabled in public.

Given that Face unlock requires only a front-facing camera, there’s absolutely no reason why Apple couldn’t also make it available on the Mac.

Face ID has been something MacBook consumers have been wanting for a great many years, and despite a decade’s worth of Apple patents for just this, it still hasn’t happened. Face unlock would be a compromise option that would at least get us some of the way there. I see I’m not the first to suggest this, with Macworld’s Roman Loyola beating me to it.

What’s your view? If you own an iPhone Duo, will you choose to enable this? If you own a MacBook, would you like the same option on that? Please take our poll and share your thoughts in the comments.

Update: Apple is reportedly about to sign a similar contract with Samsung, also permitting market-driven price increases.

SK Hynix claims that while AI continues to drive demand and growth, there is little that can be done in the short to medium term to increase supply.

Supply, on the other hand, is not keeping pace with the growth of the market. Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build latest production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.

The Register reports that SK Hynix has long-term deals with 14 tech giants for priority orders, but these allow for market-based price increases.

It has been revealed that 14 big buyers […] will collectively buy more than half of its output during 2027 and 2028, and some of them want to extend those agreements. The Korean giant doesn’t mind that because the deals include “a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers”.

In a recent development, apple is used to being in the driving seat when it comes to negotiating with suppliers, but this is not the case where memory and flash storage is concerned. Here, the shortages mean that it will have been forced to agree to contracts that allow significant price hikes in order to obtain guaranteed supplies.

Industry observers note that nikkei Asia also reports that printed circuit boards may be the next component to experience constrained supply. Once a humble commodity item, advances in the technology has turned them into specialist tech, with more layers and higher bandwidth requirements. The report says “that complexity shrinks the supplier pool and extends lead times.”.

Apple said back in June that the company was doing its best to mitigate the price increases, but it has so far been unable to do so.

There's one more vital part to the Spatial and that's the three lines on the front of the design. These are used to align the band with the center of your face, to ensure the sound is delivered to the right part of the forehead.

In a recent development, I used the Spatial Sleep Headband for four weeks as part of my usual routine, wearing it to bed (with an eye mask). Here's how I rate the performance...

Recent findings suggest that setting up the Spatial Sleep Headband is simple, for a piece of complex tech. First you have to charge it, then turn the headband on (there's a button on the front) and connect it to the app.

In a recent development, you'll be asked to scan your face — this helps Spatial create a sound just right for you. When you're ready to sleep, get the band in position and press start on the app.

According to recent reports, the sound automatically plays for 45 minutes, at which point you should be asleep (fingers crossed). You can pause and restart the sound from the app, in case of late night wake ups.

It has been revealed that the battery lasts for roughly 90 minutes, or two sessions, and I have used mine through two nights without charging. However, I recommend charging after every session, to avoid the sound cutting out. A USB-C cable is provided and charging takes roughly 30 minutes.

The app is mostly used to kick off the audio at night, but there's a fun memory game you can play as well.

Recent findings suggest that I'm normally game for testing any kind of weird sleep tech but when I first strapped the Spatial Band to my head, I felt like I'd made a terrible mistake. Nodules pressed into my forehead and my bones rattled to a dissonant hum that sounded like pans clattering to the ground in the distance. I clenched my jaw and waited for it to end.

There was an crucial lesson here, echoed in the bright red dents on my forehead: do not over-tighten the band.

With a slightly looser band, night two went better. But the first week was rough. The sound and sensations of the Spatial Headband are far removed from my usual sleep comforts. I was hoping using it would help me drift off quickly but instead I lay awake, questioning the life choices that had led me to this moment.

Spatial does warn that it takes persistence before you see results and week two went better. The sound and I had gotten used to each other, meaning it no longer sat at the forefront of my mind. Now I enjoyed a pleasant background hum and only occasionally worried about my vibrating skull.

By week three I could see a glimmer of progress. The distant drone of the sleep headband had grown relaxing. One night, on the brink of sleep, I even found myself wondering what the pleasant noise was.

Industry observers note that these benefits have yet to be reflected in my sleep score, however. On some nights it still takes me up upwards of 30 minutes to drift off fully. And I'm still experiencing brief wake ups in the night. (Including waking up to take the headband off — the nodules are uncomfortable when they press against your face.).

Industry observers note that last night, having reached the end of my four weeks testing period, I decided to ditch the headband and go back to my usual sleep patterns. I got an 88 sleep score from my Oura Ring, my highest in 12 nights.

As someone with only minor sleep problems, the Spatial Sleep Headband is a steep learning curve for a small advantage. But I don't want to write it off entirely. There are strong reviews from other customers and Spatial has conducted some notable research. Spatial is designed to improve your natural sleep frequency, so for those who have a sleep routine that's completely off-beat, the Spatial sleep might help set the pace you need.

The Spatial Headband uses acoustic vibrations and sleep-friendly frequencies to improve the quality and quantity of your sleep. It requires regular use to see the results and after several weeks the strange hum of the Spatial should be the backdrop to a decent night's rest.

In a recent development, the problem is that those first weeks are challenging, to put it mildly. From the sound to the feel, the Spatial band is simply strange to use. It feels like a disruptive force and you might be tempted to give up before you feel the benefits. Or rather, if you feel the benefits — I stuck with mine and noticed only minor differences.

In a recent development, ✅ You're experiencing long-term sleep deprivation: The Spatial Sleep Headband didn't work for me but it is backed by some serious research. Its impact might be more noticeable when overcoming bigger sleep problems.

✅ You've tried all kinds of sleep tech and nothing works: Acoustic resonance is unusual and not the kind of sleep enhancer you pick up on a whim. If you're struggling to improve your sleep, this might be worth a try.

Sources indicate that ✅ You're kept awake by disruptive noise: When the Spatial band is on, it drowns out most other sounds. That's good news if traffic or rowdy neighbors are contributing to your sleep problems.

❌ You want a quick solution: Spatial suggests it takes three to four weeks to feel the benefit of the Sleep Headband, and I found week one to be a steep learning curve. The Muse S Athena sleep headband was much easier to get used to.

❌ You share a bed with a light sleeper: Some sound does leak from the Spatial headband which might disturb co-sleepers.

Sources indicate that ❌ You want a small sleep boost, rather than a total overhaul: For minor sleep concerns the Spatial Sleep Band is a pricey investment that takes time to get used to. Try low-cost options like sleepy tea and guided meditations before diving in with the Spatial.

Industry observers note that the Muse S Athena uses your brainwaves to track your sleep and, when it senses you're about to be disturbed, plays a sleep-inducing sound to send you back under. I tested it and found the performance impressive but it is a premium buy, retailing for $479.99 at Muse and Amazon.

According to recent reports, the Snoozeband isn't as high-tech as the other options listed here but this comfortable set of sleep headphones can help you drift off in noisy environments. It utilizes thin speakers in a soft headband to deliver sleep sounds without the discomfort of an earbud. From $49.99 at Snoozeband.

Recent findings suggest that the stock market continues to grapple with volatility amid geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom. Given this uncertainty, investors looking for steady income can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios.

Tracking the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick the right dividend stocks, as these experts assign their ratings after an in-depth analysis of a company's financials and ability to pay dividends consistently.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

It has been revealed that downstream energy company Phillips 66 (PSX) is this week's first dividend pick. With a quarterly dividend $1.27 per share (annualized dividend of $5.08), PSX offers a yield of 2.25%. The company recently reported solid Q2 earnings, as the Middle East conflict affected global supplies and drove up refining margins.

Following the Q2 print, TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Phillips 66 and raised his price target to $255 from $240, reflecting higher 2026 earnings expectations and lower interest expense next year.

Sources indicate that gabelman highlighted the quarter-over-quarter reduction in Phillips 66's net debt, noting management's optimism at achieving its estimated $15.5 billion net debt target one year ahead of schedule. The 5-star analyst expects the organization to end 2026 with a net debt of $14.6 billion.

"The [balance sheet] improvement could re-establish PSX as a go-to defensive refiner," said Gabelman.

Management agreed that PSX's payout ratio lagged year-to-date, but expects buybacks to increase in the second half. Gabelman stated Phillps indicated the possibility of a larger dividend hike following an annual increase of 5% over the past two years.

Industry observers note that gabelman ranks No. 554 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 14.9%. See Phillips 66 Statistics on TipRanks.

Crescent Energy (CRGY) is an exploration and production company with activities focused in the Eagle Ford, Permian and Uinta Basins. Earlier this month, the company reported better-than-expected Q2 earnings and unveiled a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share, payable on August 31. At an annualized dividend of $0.48 per share, CRGY boasts a dividend yield of about 4%.

Industry observers note that in reaction to Q2 results, Evercore analyst Stephen Richardson reaffirmed a buy rating on Crescent Energy stock with a price target of $18. He noted continued strength in the company's performance, with second-quarter oil production and cash flow surpassing the Street's expectations.

"CRGY's cash flow exceeded expectations by 10%, reinforcing its trajectory of capital efficiency," mentioned Richardson.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that Crescent raised its full-year oil production guidance, citing the effective integration of the Vital Energy acquisition. Specifically, Crescent tripled its synergy target from the Vital Energy deal to as much as $300 million, significantly reducing the effective purchase price. This reflects Crescent's solid execution following the acquisition, Richardson said.

Additionally, the analyst noted that Crescent's capital spending is and heading toward the lower end of management's prior guidance, indicating disciplined financial controls.

Richardson ranks No. 579 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 65% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.5%. See Crescent Energy Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Finally, Viper Energy (VNOM) is effectively controlled by Diamondback Energy. Viper owns and acquires mineral and royalty interests in oil-weighted basins, mainly the Permian in West Texas. Viper recently announced its Q2 2026 results and declared a 32% hike in its base dividend, effective in the third quarter of 2026. The newly introduced base dividend indicates a 4.5% annualized yield.

Viper also removed its quarterly commitment to return at least 75% of cash available for distribution. The company believes that this move will ensure increased flexibility to make opportunistic share repurchases and pursue accretive mergers and acquisitions.

Industry observers note that following the Q2 results, TD Cowen analyst Aaron Bilkoski reiterated a buy rating on Viper, slightly raising his price target to $59 from $58. Bilkoski remarked Viper's solid Q2 performance supports his view that the strength in oil prices and rising operator activity are driving higher production.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin (BTC +0.07%) is the world's largest cryptocurrency.
  • It has been revealed that bitcoin hit a record high of $124,773 in October 2025, but it then lost more than half its value as investors slashed their exposure to volatile, speculative assets in the wake of rising economic and political uncertainty earlier this year.
  • Recent findings suggest that volatility has been a hallmark of Bitcoin investing since it introduced in 2009.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin (BTC +0.07%) is the world's largest cryptocurrency. Its market capitalization of $1.35 trillion actually represents more than half the value of all coins and tokens in circulation across the entire industry, which stands at $2.35 trillion as I write this (Nov. 14).

It has been revealed that bitcoin hit a record high of $124,773 in October 2025, but it then lost more than half its value as investors slashed their exposure to volatile, speculative assets in the wake of rising economic and political uncertainty earlier this year. The cryptocurrency recently attempted to mount a recovery and rose as high as $86,700, but it has turned lower once again, and fell below $70,000 last Friday for the first time since August.

Recent findings suggest that volatility has been a hallmark of Bitcoin investing since it introduced in 2009. The cryptocurrency has suffered two peak-to-trough declines of more than 70% over the last 10 years alone, and it recovered to set a newly introduced record high both times. Therefore, should investors treat this moment as a buying opportunity?

Bitcoin is different from most traditional assets, including stocks, bonds, real estate, and precious metals. It's entirely digital, it's fully decentralized, and it's built on a transparent system of record called the blockchain. It also has a capped supply of 21 million coins, which creates the perception of scarcity.

In a recent development, but although Bitcoin launched more than 17 years ago, people still don't fully agree on its true use case. Some believe it could transform the entire financial system and become the world's reserve currency, while others think it's a great store of value, akin to a digital version of gold. There is also a vocal group of people who think it's simply a speculative asset with no intrinsic value, and thus will eventually go to zero.

Setting the debate aside, one thing is clear: Bitcoin has outperformed every major asset class over the last 10 years by a country mile, generating a whopping 9,510% return.

According to recent reports, there is little evidence to support the idea that Bitcoin will become a widely adopted global currency. So far, just 7,266 businesses are willing to accept it in exchange for goods and services (according to Cryptwerk), and many of them are obscure providers of internet and crypto services. If the average consumer can't spend Bitcoin at their favorite stores, they simply don't have any reason to own it.

The argument that Bitcoin is a good store of value is also on shaky ground. Going back to the start of 2025, investors have dealt with the Trump administration's widespread tariffs that disrupted global trade, in addition to latest geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East that continue to roil the energy markets. They are also contending with rising interest rates and significant volatility in the stock market right now.

However, Bitcoin has actually declined by 27% in the face of all the uncertainty dating back to Jan. 1, 2025, whereas actual gold has rocketed higher by 47%. In other words, when investors need a safe-haven asset, they are making a clear choice -- and it isn't Bitcoin.

Gold Price in US Dollars data by YCharts.

In a recent development, over the last decade, Bitcoin has suffered two peak-to-trough declines of more than 70%. The first one happened between 2017 and 2018, and the second one occurred between 2021 and 2022. The cryptocurrency fully recovered and set a new high both times, and as I highlighted earlier, it has still obliterated every major asset class even after factoring in those crashes.

CRYPTO · As of 10:06 AM ET 11/17/26.

According to recent reports, however, since Bitcoin was only down by 53% at the lowest point of its 2025 to 2026 crash, there might be more downside to come. If this decline matches previous cycles and exceeds 70%, we could see a price of around $37,400 per coin (or potentially even less) before it mounts a proper recovery.

Of course, there is no guarantee Bitcoin will ever set a fresh record high. Considering some of the bullish arguments in favor of long-term upside might be losing credibility, I think the cryptocurrency will attract far fewer dip-buyers this time around.

Investors who choose to buy Bitcoin right now because they believe in its long-term potential might want to keep position sizing small in order to keep the potential risks in check. But I proposal to avoid it altogether myself.

A security researcher has discovered that some of the world’s most popular websites were compromised in an attempt to steal cryptocurrency from iPhone users.

In a recent development, A total of 178 websites were affected, including BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, and Zoom. Reasonably recent versions of iOS are safe, and so far it appears that only a few thousand dollars have been stolen ….

Reuters reports that hackers attacked Optimizely, a website optimization platform used by many major websites.

Industry observers note that several of the affected companies remarked that they have disabled the Optimizely scripts and are investigating potential impacts. Helme states almost all of the rogue code has now been removed, and that Apple patched iOS after an identical attack method was detected last month.

Industry observers note that the Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit’s own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched.

Helme monitored the attacker’s wallets and discovered that only $7,040 has been stolen, though it’s not possible to see how many payment card numbers were obtained.

As always, the best protection against this type of attack is to promptly enhancement all your Apple devices to the latest OS versions they support.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • School cellphone bans are beginning to modestly improve students’ academic performance, according to the first large national analysis that compared students’ test scores before and after the bans.
  • Industry observers note that schools with strict bans — requiring students to lock their phones in pouches all school day — saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year, the study found.
  • students’ test scores began falling over a decade ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

School cellphone bans are beginning to modestly improve students’ academic performance, according to the first large national analysis that compared students’ test scores before and after the bans.

Industry observers note that schools with strict bans — requiring students to lock their phones in pouches all school day — saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year, the study found. It was published Tuesday by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard.

U.S. students’ test scores began falling over a decade ago. The drop coincided with the rise of smartphones, raising questions about their role in the decline. The evidence so far on the academic effects of phone bans has been mixed. But the fresh study indicates they are starting to have an influence.

Sources indicate that “The earlier studies on cellphone bans have been dismissed as implying small impacts, and in-school cellphone use has been ruled out as playing a significant role in the decline,” remarked Thomas Kane, a professor at the Harvard Graduate School of Education and an author of the study. “But we think that’s mistaken.”.

The study looked at 3.3 million students between 2021 and 2026. They were in third through 10th grade, attending 4,600 U.S. schools. Using scores on MAP tests, which track achievement from fall to spring, it compared the performance of students at schools that put in strict phone bans with those at similar schools that did not have such bans.

The annual gains reversed about half the annual loss that an average student experienced in the years leading up to the pandemic. (Students lost even more ground during pandemic closures.).

Disney has declared a major milestone coming next month in its looks to merge the Disney+ and Hulu apps, which will be “fully unified” into Disney+ soon.

Today Disney reported its quarterly earnings and gave an update on aims to merge Disney+ and Hulu into one app.

Live TV and premium add-ons were the final Hulu features that hadn’t yet been imported to the Disney+ app. But by adding those capabilities into Disney+, the app unification will be “complete.”.

The ultimate goal of unifying everything in Disney+, though, will be accomplished soon.

Sources indicate that also in the earnings report, Disney said that creator content will start appearing in the Disney+ app in December. This is related to the manufacturer’s deal with TikTok that debuted after its previous OpenAI deal fell apart when Sora was killed off. The Disney+ app will also get “more vertical video, live sports, and podcasts” soon too, Disney said.

Recent findings suggest that what do you think of the intends for the Disney+ app? Let us know in the comments.

AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.
  • Data centers already use light in networking.
  • The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

Data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” notes Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Sources indicate that optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

Sources indicate that “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” notes Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in Newly introduced Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

Industry observers note that inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Recent findings suggest that back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon notes this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also notable to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is presently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.
