The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.

According to recent reports, the startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the manufacturer’s tech to beat GPUs.

It has been revealed that instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr indicates.

Industry observers note that to accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.

Sources indicate that the Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.

In a recent development, lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.

It has been revealed that the startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the tech giant is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.

“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” states Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”.

Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.

Industry observers note that bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.

Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”.

Industry observers note that the approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The firm is at the moment choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr claims. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”.

Recent findings suggest that free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another major advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” claims Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”.

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” states Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”.

Sources indicate that one way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the company unveiled a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

According to recent reports, the energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main matter is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch claims, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”.

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

“A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” indicates Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”.

Industry observers note that even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the tech giant believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says.

The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” indicates Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the company’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

It has been revealed that lightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver.

In a recent development, lightSolver’s team is at the moment working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the firm’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

Yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” New indicates. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”.

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick Latest, Optalysis.

According to recent reports, instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

Recent findings suggest that some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

Latest indicates that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”.

Recent findings suggest that how likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he notes. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”.

However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Says Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”.

It has been revealed that whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [neural processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”.

#16100. We don't need more apps. We need better open source

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (548 w)

We don't need more apps. We need better open source

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (548 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jordankrueger

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every day, a dozen people post a new app they built with AI over a weekend: a habit tracker, a to-do list, another note-taking app.
  • But far less of that energy goes into the open source software we already rely on.
  • People call this newly introduced way of building “vibecoding.” I hate the name; it makes a real shift in who gets to write software sound like a joke.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every day, a dozen people post a new app they built with AI over a weekend: a habit tracker, a to-do list, another note-taking app. I’m glad! More people building things is one of the best parts of this moment.

But far less of that energy goes into the open source software we already rely on.

People call this newly introduced way of building “vibecoding.” I hate the name; it makes a real shift in who gets to write software sound like a joke. I’ll call it AI-assisted coding, and I think it could aim somewhere more useful.

Free and open source software already does most of what my clients and I need. What it often can’t do is run well on a cheap server, install in one step, or stay up without forum threads at 11pm.

Industry observers note that I self-host a lot of my own stuff, and I help progressive nonprofits with their tech for a living. I run a Matrix server (Synapse, Element and a moderation bot) for a community with thousands of users. I also run apps on Coolify and Hetzner, keep my paperwork in Paperless-ngx, and own a Mac Mini that’s always one download from a full disk.

According to recent reports, the software is usually great. Running it is the hard part. Install guides assume you know five other tools. Upgrades break things. Apps eat 4GB of RAM to serve a handful of people. Error messages tell you nothing.

My nonprofit clients would love to leave Substantial Tech for privacy, cost and owning their data. But the open source option usually needs a part-time sysadmin they don’t have, so they pay for the corporate tool.

A upcoming to-do app usually helps the few people who find it. Making a tool millions already use 20% lighter helps all of them, every day.

This is also the work that slides when maintainers are tired, and many are unpaid volunteers. We saw the risk in 2024. Someone spent years earning the trust of the worn-out solo maintainer of xz, a compression tool inside most Linux systems, then slipped a backdoor into it.

I think this unglamorous work suits AI well: profiling slow code, writing tests that make big changes safe, testing installers, rewriting cryptic errors, writing the missing docs. It takes patience more than brilliance, plus a person who checks every line.

It matters politically too. If organizations are going to own their data instead of renting it from a few giant companies, open source has to be something a 20-person nonprofit can run. I want AI’s gains shared widely. Better public tools that anyone can use, change and share are one way to get there.

Maintainers have already seen the wrong way. The curl project ended its bug bounty in January 2026 after a flood of fake, AI-generated security reports. By April, its lead developer wrote that the fakes were mostly gone and almost every report used AI, most of them very good. The latest problem is volume. Even good work can bury a maintainer. So:.

Pick one open source tool you use. Find the most annoying thing about installing or running it. Spend a weekend fixing it, with the people who maintain it. Then tell me about it.

How to hide the upcoming macOS 27.3 menu bar indicator

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (332 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override.
  • If you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar.
  • I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override. Apple describes itas a transparency indicator that appears when one app is controlling another.

If you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar. Prefer to hide it? There’s a Terminal workaround.

I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.

Open Terminal and run these two commands:.

sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domainsudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR -dict Enabled -bool false.

Enter your Mac administrator password when prompted, then restart your Mac.

Industry observers note that the command disables the internal AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR feature flag. It doesn’t remove apps from your permissions list, although you’ll no longer see this activity indicator.

To restore Apple’s default behavior, run:.

sudo defaults delete /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR.

Restart your Mac again to apply the reversal. This removes only the indicator override, preserving any other flags you may have configured.

This is an undocumented workaround tested on the current beta, so Apple could change or remove it in a future enhancement.

Recent findings suggest that not a fan of this on macOS 27.3 beta 2. #16095. Industry News: I found a hidden Android tool that solves all my tiny text troubles

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (656 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: I found a hidden Android tool that solves all my tiny text troubles

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How many times have you been on your phone, wanted to read something (a piece of news, a website, etc.), only to find the text is too small and every effort to zoom in doesn’t work?
  • Also: 7 Android accessibility features that can make your life easier.
  • This happens quite often when I’m viewing content in the Google News app — especially in the morning, when my eyes are still in “wake up” mode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How many times have you been on your phone, wanted to read something (a piece of news, a website, etc.), only to find the text is too small and every effort to zoom in doesn’t work?

Also: 7 Android accessibility features that can make your life easier.

This happens quite often when I’m viewing content in the Google News app — especially in the morning, when my eyes are still in “wake up” mode. It can be frustrating. And it’s not only text. Sometimes there’s an image I need to enlarge, but for whatever reason, pinch-to-zoom isn’t working on that particular screen.

Industry observers note that fortunately, there’s an option you can enable to ensure you can always zoom in on your Android device, no matter what’s on the screen. The option is found in Accessibility and is aptly called Magnification. With this feature enabled, you can promptly zoom in on the screen to enlarge any displayed content. It doesn’t matter what’s on the screen or what app is showing the image, page, or text — Magnification will magnify it.

This iteration of the feature has been available since Android 15. I found it by accident while poking around the Settings page. Since then, I’ve used it quite a bit, and it’s eased my morning frustration with reading news sites.

Industry observers note that the Magnification feature is quite simple: once enabled, a magnifier shortcut appears on the screen. Tap that button, and whatever is on your screen will increase in size. It’s really that easy. One caveat: As long as the Magnification shortcut is enabled, the button remains on your screen. You can move the button up and down or to the left or right side of the display, but if you want the feature enabled, the button must remain.

Industry observers note that the good news, however, is that the button does fade a bit, so it’s not glaring and in your face. You can still see it, but it gets just enough transparency that it doesn’t stand out all that much.

Also: Android is getting my favorite iOS tracking feature.

OK, let’s enable Magnification.

Open Settings by dragging the Notification Shade down twice, then tapping the gear icon (or tapping Settings in the App Drawer). Where this is located depends on the Android version you’re using and your device. For example, on my Pixel 9 Pro, it’s in Settings > Accessibility > Magnification. On a RedMagic 12 Pro, it’s in Settings > Features > Accessibility. If you don’t find it right away, open Settings and search for Magnification.

Once you’ve found the Magnification option, tap the On/Off slider until it’s in the On position, and the Magnifier button will appear on your screen. Tap the button, and whatever is on the display will enlarge enough that you shouldn’t have any trouble reading it.

Here’s a little tip: After tapping the Magnification button, whatever’s been enlarged can be scrolled vertically, but not horizontally. Fortunately, there’s a way to ensure that you can read everything on the page.

Also: I use Google Magnifier to read tiny print without my glasses.

Tap the gear icon at the bottom right of the display to open the options pop-up. On this page, tap the “Magnifier size” icon that’s second from the right. This enables a movable magnifier you can place where you need it (kind of like a traditional magnifying glass). You can also change the size of the movable magnifier (by tapping one of the other “Magnifier size” buttons) as well as the size of the text when magnified (by dragging the bottom slider).

Also: RedMagic 12 Pro is the fastest Android phone I’ve ever seen.

This feature has alleviated the early-morning frustration of having to squint (even with my glasses on) to read certain news sites. Give it a try and see if it doesn’t make your Android life a bit clearer.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, google and Xreal's spatial computing AR glasses have finally arrived and I've been wearing them for just a few days.
  • According to recent reports, in the smart glasses space, there isn't anything like the Aura's.
  • Xreal's only potential rivals exist in tech that has yet to actually hit shelves: the Snap Specs (which are supposed to ship "this fall") and the Meta VR Glasses that don't drop until sometime in Spring 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, google and Xreal's spatial computing AR glasses have finally arrived and I've been wearing them for just a few days. They're an interesting hint at the future of both computing and wearables.

According to recent reports, in the smart glasses space, there isn't anything like the Aura's. They're not quite a VR headset, but they're far more advanced than display glasses like Xreal's own One Pro Plus.

Xreal's only potential rivals exist in tech that has yet to actually hit shelves: the Snap Specs (which are supposed to ship "this fall") and the Meta VR Glasses that don't drop until sometime in Spring 2027.

Sources indicate that there's a lot going on here, and we'll have a full review soon, but here are some early first impressions. As we dig into the glasses, if there's something you want to know reach out to scott.younker@futurenet.com or leave a comment below!

Recent findings suggest that beyond the puck, the Xreal Aura glasses won't look out of place next to any other display spectacles made by the company. There is an aesthetic to this kind of glasses and you can see it mirrored in Xreal's rival Viture with the recent Pro 2 glasses.

In a recent development, where you'll notice the difference is in the cameras. Like the best smart glasses, the Aura features cameras at the temples plus one on the nose bridge. These are built to enable the gesture controls and 6DoF spatial computing, something no other Xreal glasses have natively.

In a recent development, the Aura sits somewhat between Meta's VR Glasses and Snap Specs; mostly, it comes down to software and cameras. Meta glasses have more cameras that can "see" your hands even if they're in your lap.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

With the Aura's, moving your hands down to your lap means you're most likely using the puck as a trackpad, which works pretty well.

The puck is a computer for the glasses thanks to the powerful Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset. If you work in the Google suite, you have access to all of the Google apps and services you could want. Plus, it comes with Gemini AI, which you can access via voice controls.

In a recent development, nicely, you don't need the puck for mirroring. You can connect the glasses to any device, save the Switch 2 (more on that below), and they will work like your normal Xreal glasses.

According to recent reports, if you've worn a pair of Xreal glasses, the Aura feels about the same. I think they're fairly comfortable, and they do come with different nose pad sizes. Plus, the arms can be adjusted by three levels, which helps settle the glasses.

I want to highlight the speakers in the Aura. I hate speakers in display glasses and often find them tinny, preferring to use headphones. Also, especially since I travel or use the glasses to not disturb my partner at night even if the speakers are siloed, sound still leaks out.

Now, the Bose speakers in the Aura won't beat the best headphones, but they sound way better than any other glasses I've tested.

The included puck has both the computing chipsets and the battery. The puck is about the size of a thick iPhone 16, and does have some heft. You could use the included belt clip so that you don't have to hold the puck when you're out and about (which gives cellphone belt guy vibes).

The Xreal Aura are rated for about 3 hours of continuous use. I haven't done a full rundown test yet, but in my usage I've found that to be fairly accurate.

Perhaps that's for the best. I've found that the portion of the glasses that rests on your eyebrows gets warm. Not uncomfortably so, but noticeably enough that I wonder how that settles out over the long term. The puck, however, does seem to dissipate heat fairly well, and I never felt it get warm.

It has been revealed that xreal partnered with Google on the Aura and you can feel Mountain View's presence in the Android XR platform that lives in the puck. If you've ever tested the Samsung Galaxy XR headset, then you've seen the Android XR interface before.

In a recent development, it's the exact same here, with fewer capabilities thanks to fewer cameras and a little less power. The Aura also has a smaller FOV of 70 degrees. VR enthusiasts won't like that, but I think most people will find it more than usable.

You can use pinch gestures or the trackpad puck to control the interface. So far I've found the gesture controls smooth and intuitive. The Aura comes with a delightful setup process that teaches you how to use the gesture controls and puck so you can open the glasses up ready to go. It's honestly one of the better startup tutorials I've come across.

In previous hands-on sessions, the gesture controls felt a bit laggy at times, but whatever work Xreal and Google have done in the meantime has really made the controls much better.

Honestly, it's not as exciting as the eye-tracking in the Meta VR Glasses, but it works well, so I'm not knocking it too much.

In a recent development, since the system runs on Android XR there are a lot of AR (and some VR-lite) games that you can play on the Aura. Xreal recommended the excellent Demeo, which is available in the Play Store.

I've already enjoyed Demeo in VR and the AR translation is a delight, using pinch controls to move the map, zoom in, and make choices. You'll need to pay attention to your hand position so the cameras can catch it.

Sources indicate that I do think you'll need a controller to enjoy the most out of what the Aura can do or a mouse and keyboard. Fortunately, you can connect a surprising number of accessories to the Aura via Bluetooth (more on that below).

Sources indicate that but what makes the Aura standout is the connectivity. As mentioned, you can just use the glasses to run a Steam Deck or mirror using a cable on your laptop. Have I been running WoW: Forever through the Aura glasses? Yes. Should I? That remains to be seen.

We got a sneak peek during AWE 2026 back in June, but the Xreal Aura is one of the few glasses that can connect to the Switch 2. Compared to the mini dock and larger pro dock that Viture makes, the Aura puck is lighter, smaller and does more than just act as a passthrough and battery pack. And it does so through the USB-C connection into the puck.

It's a delight to pop in Mario Kart World or the Ocarina of Time remake on the glasses. I still don't know how Xreal and Qualcomm got this to work, but I'm happy it does.

Recent findings suggest that xreal has mentioned that you can accessorize the Aura with peripherals to enhance your use. With that in mind, the tech giant did send us a wireless gaming controller built by GameSir, a wireless folding keyboard and a USB-C DP-in for mirroring external devices.

All three add an extra cost on top of the initial $1,299 glasses price. The GameSir controller costs $99 and can be used wirelessly or wired and has an AI button.

GameSir makes good controllers and the Xreal one is pretty decent. However, if you already have an Xbox, PlayStation or other Bluetooth controller, the Aura will support them. You won't have the Gemini button, but if you're like me and don't use that anyway, it shouldn't be a problem.

The Xreal keyboard is $79 but comes with Aura-specific keys in the FN row that enable you to control the glasses like you would your monitor on a laptop. It's actually a pretty comfortable keyboard, and the foldability for travel makes it an excellent companion. Honestly, so far you should add the $79 as part of the cost of getting a pair of Auras. You can also pair it with other devices, including laptops and tablets.

It has been revealed that the cable is a Silkland USB-C one that costs $12.99. If you already have a USB-C DP in cable, it should work, but you're not out too much if you're looking to do wired mirroring.

At over $1,000, the Xreal Aura is pretty expensive, but these glasses are a lot of compute shrunk down into a pair of glasses and a cell phone-sized puck.

I don't know that everyone needs these glasses, and it's not quite the super portable laptop replacement yet, but it is an exciting glimpse at the future of AR glasses. Between the Aura, Snap Specs, and Meta VR Glasses the next generation of glasses has some true potential.

There's also room for the Aura to grow from both a software and hardware perspective.

We're not there yet, but the Aura feels like a true step toward the sci-fi eyewear that we saw in movies and highlights as kids.

Need more AI in Creator Studio? Apple may charge you for it

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there are plenty of AI subscriptions out there, but Apple’s AI features are among the few still accessible by simply purchasing a device.
  • Apple is introducing a one-time purchase option for AI Usage Packs via app updates to Creator Studio.
  • Google AI Pro: Two $20 aims, very different perks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there are plenty of AI subscriptions out there, but Apple’s AI features are among the few still accessible by simply purchasing a device. Now, Apple is shifting its business model by offering a one-time $50 purchase option to grant server-based AI capacity in some apps, starting with Creator Studio apps.

Apple is introducing a one-time purchase option for AI Usage Packs via app updates to Creator Studio. If you want expanded access to AI features in Final Cut Pro, Pixelmator Pro, the iWork Suite, and Logic Pro, you’ll need to pay.

Also: ChatGPT Plus vs. Google AI Pro: Two $20 aims, very different perks.

The $50 fee applies to extra usage blocks and kicks in when you exceed predetermined limits in these apps. Instead of a recurring fee, Apple is hoping the one-time fee for intelligence usage packs will help the firm offset some of the cost of AI. Consumers can buy a pack for Logic Pro now, and the other apps are expected to get it soon.

“Usage Packs may offer the option to prepay for the use of certain AI-based Services and represent the amount you have paid in advance for use of the respective Services,” according to Apple.

Apple’s one-time payment breaks away from what most companies are doing. Most companies offering AI tools try to offset the steep cost of running large language models (LLMs) by charging consumers for paid subscriptions. For example, Samsung is rumored to be planning such a subscription for Galaxy AI usage, including access to features that are at the moment free.

Also: The best tablets of 2026: Lab-tested recommendations.

In a recent development, the Creator Studio apps are the only ones getting the Usage Packs for now. The legal terms for intelligence Usage Packs explain that these packs would be available in “AI apps,” which include not only Final Cut Pro, Compressor, Logic Pro, MainStage, Pixelmator Pro, Motion, but also Pages, Keynote, Numbers, Freeform, and other apps.

You’re not required to purchase the Usage Packs to enjoy the core functionality of the apps in the Creator Studio. However, the fact that the Usage Packs are to be applied to popular apps like Pages and Freeform begs the question of whether Apple intends to put a paywall on features that are presently free.

Recent findings suggest that some of the features for which you may be required to purchase Usage Packs once you exceed your limits include the generation of images, shapes, presentations, and presenter notes, as well as some assistant features. Usage limits reset each month.

Also: Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Forget everything you knew about Amazon tablets.

You can view your usage status for each of the applicable apps on your iPhone or iPad by tapping on More (or the button with three dots), then Intelligence Features, and Show Usage Status. On a Mac, it’s available by accessing Intelligence Features from the menu bar of the app you’re using, then clicking on Show Usage Status.

Intelligence usage packs expire after 12 months, but they roll over each month if left unused.

#16088. Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited

📖 Baca

Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, windows 11 customers who’ve struggled to navigate and use the right-click menu in File Explorer now finally have some relief.
  • It has been revealed that as usual, the monthly patch is mandatory, which means it should automatically download and install on your PC.
  • Also: You can change Windows settings directly from a search now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, windows 11 customers who’ve struggled to navigate and use the right-click menu in File Explorer now finally have some relief. With the November Patch Tuesday Windows update, you’re now able to customize the menu to add and remove specific commands and apps so that only your favorites appear.

It has been revealed that as usual, the monthly patch is mandatory, which means it should automatically download and install on your PC. To check, head to Settings and select Windows Update. If the latest update — labeled “2026-11 Security Update (KB5132061) (26300.9974)” -– pops up as installed with a pending restart, just reboot your computer. Otherwise, click the button to check for updates and allow it to download and install.

Also: You can change Windows settings directly from a search now.

One caveat: Microsoft’s monthly updates fully support Windows 11 26H2 and 25H2. But support for 24H2 ended last month, at least for the Home and Pro editions. Windows 11 24H2 Enterprise and Education will continue to get monthly security updates, though not regular non-security preview updates, while Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise and Education will receive no more updates after this month.

If you use Windows 11 Home or Pro, be sure you upgrade your system to 26H2 to continue receiving the necessary support and updates.

First and foremost in the latest revision is the upcoming customizable right-click menu.

Recent findings suggest that the context-sensitive right-click menu is a handy way to quickly access key settings, features, and apps, both in File Explorer and on the desktop. But there’s always been a flaw in its basic design. The more apps you install, the more cluttered and disorganized the menu becomes. That was especially problematic in previous versions of Windows. The old-style, classic menu would grow so long that it would be difficult to navigate and let you find the item you wanted.

According to recent reports, with Windows 11, Microsoft introduced a more modern and pared-down menu. But this version can also get crowded. Plus, it may not display every command you need, so you often have to revert to the older classic menu. You’re then stuck dealing with two separate versions of the same menu, leading to an even more confusing and cumbersome experience.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now, Microsoft states.

Industry observers note that the ideal solution is a menu that you can customize yourself, and that’s what we now have, at least that’s what is now rolling out. Microsoft calls this one a gradual rollout, which means you may or may not get it right away.

It has been revealed that to see if and how this is available, open File Explorer and right-click on a folder or file. If the new menu has reached your PC, you’ll see an entry for Customize menu. Select that to view all the available options for tweaking it. Alternatively, head to Settings, select Personalization, and then click the entry for Context menu.

There, you’re able to turn certain file actions on or off, such as Send to, Print, Create shortcut, Copy as path, and Rotate image. You can also choose which apps appear all the time, either in the main menu or in a submenu. Plus, additional options let you decide where certain commands and actions appear and whether you can still access the old-style menu.

Though the customizable right-click menu is the star of the update, Microsoft has added other surprises as it strives to make Windows more reliable and user-friendly.

Recent findings suggest that also gradually rolling out, Cloud rebuild is a new recovery option that lets you reinstall Windows 11 via cloud-based system images and drivers downloaded from Windows Revision. This tool can help you recover Windows when it won’t load and you don’t have a USB drive or your own custom image. The downside is that your files won’t survive. But if you regularly back them up as you should, you can restore them after Windows is back in business.

To start Cloud rebuild, go to Settings, select System, click Recovery, and then select Rebuild PC. Your PC will then restart into the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) to kick off the cloud rebuild. If Windows can load, your computer should automatically enter WinRE mode, where you can then choose the cloud rebuild. You should need to make sure your PC is online via a wired or wireless connection.

The November enhancement also enhances or fixes other Windows features and apps.

Recent findings suggest that file Explorer will now more clearly and consistently show you the names, locations, and dates of files when you search for them. Phone Link will preview the text in a recent message if you hover over it. The AutoPlay dialog box that appears when you connect a device like a phone or camera has been given a more modern makeover. The Privacy & security page in Settings now groups together related controls for easier viewing. Plus, there are changes to the Taskbar, Magnifier, Narrator, Xbox Mode, and Live Captions.

And that then brings us to the security fixes.

This month’s update resolves 1,094 security vulnerabilities, according to Microsoft, with 63 of them rated critical and one already exploited in the wild. That’s fewer than October’s record of 1,400 patches. But it still represents a hefty number as Microsoft and other vendors continue to rely on AI to find and fix security holes.

Also: Windows finally gets a built-in internet speed test tool – how to try it.

Though labeled Moderate, the exploited flaw points to a serious spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook. Here, a remote attacker who sends you a malicious email and convinces you to open it could cause Outlook to connect to a network controlled by that attacker. In this case, though, you would not receive any warning. Further, the exploit might reveal your username and password to the sender, potentially allowing them to impersonate you.

“An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and gets the user to open it,” Jack Bicer, Director of Vulnerability Research at patch management provider Action1, stated in an advisory.

Industry observers note that “Outlook then connects to a network location the attacker controls, but it skips the usual warning about external content,” Bicer explained further. “That quiet connection can leak the user’s NTLMv2 hash, a scrambled form of their login secret, which the attacker can use to sign in as that person. It affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024. Attackers are already exploiting it, it needs only one click on an email file, and it hits Outlook, which nearly every organization runs.”.
